1.title: A Guest from Exeter
1.description: Six months of letters from Exeter have been civil and exact. Mr Hawkins has bought you a house at Purfleet, called Carfax, with a ruined chapel in its grounds and a private asylum on the other side of the wall. His junior partner is coming to settle the deeds. Jonathan Harker comes up the pass in the last of the light in a calèche, with a stranger in a long cloak on the box and wolves keeping pace along the ridge. You are the stranger. You keep no servants, so you drove him yourself. Now you stand in the courtyard with a lamp in your hand. You have not needed a man from England so badly, or let one in.

options.label: Receive him as a host receives an honoured friend.
options.detail: Carry his bags, lay the table, pour the wine. Say that you have dined.

quote.speaker: The Count
quote.text: I am Dracula; and I bid you welcome, Mr. Harker, to my house. Come in; the night air is chill, and you must need to eat and rest.

options.outcome: You carry his bags up the stair yourself and set a table for one. He is tired and grateful, and he asks no questions that night. You learn the first thing about him: he writes down everything.

options.label: Receive him correctly and keep your distance.
options.detail: A solicitor's client, not a friend. Say little and be seen to do so.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: He was perfectly civil and perfectly cold. I wrote to Mr Hawkins that the Count seemed an old-fashioned man.

options.outcome: You give him the east room, a fire, and a cold supper, and you withdraw at once. He writes to Exeter before he sleeps. The letter says what you wanted it to say.

options.label: Meet his eyes in the doorway and make him forget the road.
options.detail: The wolves, the blue lights on the pass, the old woman at Bistritz who gave him a crucifix. He should arrive with none of it.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I remember the drive as a very long one, and a very quiet one, and I cannot say why I am so tired.

success.outcome: He blinks, smiles and sets down his bag. Whatever he saw on the road is gone from his face. He eats, and sleeps, and in the morning he remembers a pleasant journey. His own mind is easy to read now, like a letter left open on a desk.

failure.outcome: His eyes slide off yours and go to his collar, where the old woman's crucifix hangs. He puts a hand over it. You step back into the lamplight and say that the night is cold. He does not take the cross off, then or later.

2.title: What the Solicitor Knows
2.description: For a week you do what you have done for centuries by other means: you read. The library has Bradshaw's railway guide, a London directory, Whitaker's Almanack, the Army and Navy List and a shelf of English law. What the books do not give you is how an Englishman thinks, and Harker is the first one you have kept in the house. In the evenings you put your questions to him over the fire, a dozen a night. You have a month before the boxes sail, which is time to learn one subject well and the rest badly.

options.label: The law: title, lease, survey, and what a solicitor can be made to overlook.
options.detail: Learn how an English house is bought, leased and searched, so that yours can be kept shut against a warrant.

quote.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quote.text: First, he asked if a man in England might have two solicitors or more.

options.outcome: He explains the Land Registry, the searches, and the wording of a lease that no clerk will question. You write it all down in a neat, old-fashioned hand.

options.label: The manner: how an Englishman greets, dresses, dines and lies.
options.detail: Forks, bows and vowels. Harker corrects you each evening and does not ask why you need it.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: You have it almost perfectly, Count, but you would never say 'good day' after four o'clock.

options.outcome: Over a fortnight he corrects your vowels, your bow, and the order in which you take up your forks. By the end he is correcting himself.

options.label: The city: the streets, the Thames, the tide tables and the docks.
options.detail: The streets, the docks and the tide tables, from a man who has seen London from a clerk's stool.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I have lived in Exeter all my life, Count, but I have been to London often enough to be a poor guide and a good clerk.

options.outcome: He draws you the map from memory, with the tides from Bradshaw in the margin and the cab fares from his own pocket-book. Before he sleeps he has told you where a man may walk after dark without being asked what he is doing.

options.label: Whom to avoid: the doctors, the clergy, and the police.
options.detail: Ask Harker about doctors, priests and policemen. He will tell you what each does about a stranger, and wonder why you ask.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: A doctor will call if a neighbour is ill, Count. A clergyman will call if one is not.

options.outcome: He tells you, without understanding why you wish to know, which sort of man to expect at the door and what each will do about a stranger who keeps odd hours. He tells you about the asylum next to Carfax. He says its doctor is young, and inquisitive.

3.title: The Looking-Glass
3.description: In the third week Harker shaves at the window with a small glass hung on the shutter. You come into the room behind him and he does not hear you. In the glass there is the window, the room and Harker's own back, and nothing standing behind him. The crucifix at his throat catches the lamp. He starts, the razor slips, and a thread of blood runs down his chin into the soap. You have not fed in nine days.

options.label: Take the glass from him and break it, and say that you allow none in the house.
options.detail: Fury is quick, and he will believe it. He will also remember it.

quote.speaker: The Count
quote.text: It is a foul bauble of man's vanity. Away with it!

options.outcome: The glass goes through the window and lands in the courtyard. Harker stands holding a razor and a towel and looking at your face. You say that mirrors are a vanity and that a man may cut himself on them. He says that of course that is so.

options.label: Say good morning, and see that every mirror is out of the house by evening.
options.detail: Say nothing of the glass and take every mirror out of the house. He will think you vain, or odd.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: He had no looking-glass in any room but mine, and by evening mine was gone. I told myself that the house was old.

options.outcome: You keep your eyes on his face and off his chin. You wish him good morning, remark on the weather, and have every glass out of every room before dark. Harker says nothing and keeps his collar buttoned.

options.label: Step back out of the room, and keep away from the blood.
options.detail: You have not fed in nine days, and there is blood on his chin. Be on the stair before he turns.

quote.speaker: You
quote.text: A man is a guest in your house, and you are a very old host. That was the only thing you held on to.

options.outcome: You are on the stair before he has turned round. You stand there for a long time with your back to the wall. When you come down at dusk you are very civil, and he is a little afraid of you, and does not know why.

echoes.text: Harker has begun to think of you as a friend, and says so.
Harker thinks you an old-fashioned man, and has written so to Exeter.

4.title: Three Letters
4.description: Harker wants to go home. He has been a month in the castle, Hawkins expects word, and a solicitor who does not come back from a client causes questions in Exeter. You need him in the house until the boxes are ready, and you need Exeter to read nothing alarming while he is here. The simplest remedy is paper. Three letters, dated a week apart, each saying that he is well and will be home shortly, will buy you the month.

options.label: Make him write three letters, each saying he is well and will come soon.
options.detail: He is obliging. He does not see why you would ask, and he does not ask.

quote.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quote.text: I am surely in the toils.

options.outcome: He writes the first with a steady hand and the second with a shorter one, and the third on the last night of the month in a handwriting that does not look like his. You post them from Bistritz by a Slovak who has been paid not to wonder.

options.label: Write them yourself, in his hand, from the one letter of his you have.
options.detail: Copy his hand from the one letter you have. If Exeter spots a wrong capital, they will write to Bucharest.

quote.speaker: Mr Hawkins
quote.text: Harker's hand has changed a little. It is the sort of change that travel makes.

success.outcome: The first letter reaches Exeter and is read aloud at the breakfast table. Exeter remarks on nothing. The second is shown to a bank manager and the third to a niece. You have stopped needing Harker for anything but the walls.

failure.outcome: Mr Hawkins holds the second letter up to the window. He says the capitals are wrong. By the time the third arrives he has written to the British consul at Bucharest. The consul is slow, and his reply is polite, but it is on its way.

options.label: Let him write what he likes, and read every word before it leaves.
options.detail: Read every line before it goes. A clever man may hide a message in the margin.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I put a line in shorthand in the margin of the second, in case Mina or Mr Hawkins should look at it closely.

success.outcome: You find the line in the margin, in a shorthand you can read as easily as English. You say nothing. You cross it out, hand him a fresh sheet and wait while he copies the letter without it. He does not remember writing it.

failure.outcome: The second letter has a line in shorthand in the margin, and you do not look at the margin. It is on its way to Bistritz in the Slovak's coat before you see it. In Exeter, someone will remember that Harker's fiancée can read shorthand.

echoes.text: He has forgotten the wolves on the road. It makes him a better correspondent.
The shutter of the east room still shows where the glass went through.
There is not a mirror left in the house. Harker has stopped mentioning it.

5.title: The Three Sisters
5.description: Harker has wandered, against your word, into the old east wing and fallen asleep on a sofa. You know it before you see it, as you know a door has been opened in a house. When you reach the room the three who live in the east wing are already standing round him: one fair, two dark, all of them smiling. One of them has bent down to his throat. You have not seen them so eager for a long time. They turn to you, and they are not afraid.

options.label: Order them back. He is yours, and not until you say.
options.detail: They have never been refused in this house. Expect a grudge.

quote.speaker: The Count
quote.text: Back, I tell you all! This man belongs to me!

options.outcome: They go, one at a time, with looks that you will remember. The fair one laughs on the stair. Saying no costs you more than you had thought it would, and you stand over him until dawn.

options.label: Take them out hunting on the hill pastures tonight, to turn them from the house.
options.detail: Feed them on the shepherds of the high farms. It will be talked about in the village.

quote.speaker: A Sister
quote.text: Hill mutton and moonlight. Very well. You are generous tonight.

options.outcome: You take them up through the snow to the high farms, where the flocks are large and the shepherds are few. They are cheerful all the way home. In the morning two shepherds will talk about wolves, and Harker will sleep until noon.

options.label: Tell them to wait. He will be theirs when your business is done.
options.detail: Promise him to them for later. It costs nothing tonight, and it will be asked for.

quote.speaker: A Sister
quote.text: When you are done with him. We shall wait. We have always been very good at it.

options.outcome: They bow, almost mockingly, and go. They will remember the promise and so will you. There will come a night when the sisters expect to be paid.

6.title: Fifty Boxes
6.description: In the chapel crypt lie fifty chests of your own country's earth. Wherever you rest in England you will need it: a hundred hours of sleep in foreign ground is a poor sleep. The Szgany will carry the chests down the pass, Slovaks will take them on to Varna, and a Russian schooner called the Demeter will take them from there. Every box is a bed, a lair, and a thing that can be found. A hold of fifty is hard to hide. A hold of twenty is easy to lose.

options.label: Take all fifty, in one hold.
options.detail: Fifty beds across London. A hunter will have fifty boxes to find, and you will have fifty to guard.

quote.speaker: Slovak headman
quote.text: Fifty, master. It is a great deal of earth for a man who owns a mountain.

options.outcome: The Slovaks load the wagons for three nights. The headman asks nothing, because he has been paid for not asking, and because he has seen the three in the east wing. The last wagon goes down the pass at dawn.

options.label: Take forty, and leave ten in the crypt for a way home.
options.detail: Ten stay sealed in the castle crypt, a way home if England goes badly.

quote.speaker: Slovak headman
quote.text: Ten left, master? Then we shall come back for them if the master wishes, or the wolves may sit on them.

options.outcome: Forty boxes go down the pass. Ten are sealed behind the crypt door and the key is hung on a nail in your own room. You will be glad of the nail, one day, in a country where no one has a key to anywhere.

options.label: Take twenty only, light and quick, and easy to hide.
options.detail: Fewer beds to defend and a smaller cargo to explain. Thirty boxes stay here.

quote.speaker: Slovak headman
quote.text: Twenty? It will be a quick sail. But master, a man sleeps better with a spare bed.

options.outcome: Twenty is a number a harbourmaster does not remember. You will have fewer lairs and fewer things to protect. The other thirty stay in the crypt, behind a door that England will never open.

7.title: Mr Harker's Last Night
7.description: The wagons have gone down the pass. Tomorrow the castle will hold only the three in the east wing and one man locked in the north room. He has written his letters and seen more than he understands. He has also, in the evenings, told you about the people he loves: his employer, his employer's friends, and a young woman called Mina who types, writes shorthand and keeps a journal. Before you go, you have to decide what to do with a man who knows your name.

options.label: Leave him locked in the north room, with the key where he can find it in a day or two.
options.detail: The key hangs where a clever man can reach it, and the wolves are called off. He may leave, or not.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I heard the carts go. I heard him go. I do not know why I was still alive in the morning.

options.outcome: You lock the door and hang the key on a nail where it can be reached from the window with a long enough rod. You go down to the crypt without looking back. By the time he finds the key, you will be a hundred miles away.

options.label: Unlock his door, call off the wolves, and leave the road open.
options.detail: He wants to go home, and he will tell Exeter everything he has seen.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: I walked out at dawn and nobody stopped me. I did not know what to make of it. I still do not.

options.outcome: You call off the wolves in a word and leave the north room open. The sisters are asleep in the east wing and will not wake until dusk. He will have a whole day. You pay for him, in some coin that you cannot name, and you do not look for the reason.

options.label: Finish it. Nobody should be left to read what he wrote.
options.detail: Hawkins will ask after him within the month. The sisters will be fed.

quote.speaker: Mr Hawkins
quote.text: Harker has not written in six weeks. I begin to be very uneasy. I shall write to the consul.

options.outcome: You do not describe it afterwards, even to yourself. In the morning the north room is empty and the bed is made, and the castle is quiet. Hawkins will write to Bucharest in a month, and no letter will be answered.

echoes.text: He still has the old woman's crucifix at his throat. You cannot look at it for long.
Mr Hawkins has written to the British consul at Bucharest about a handwriting. The consul has not yet answered.
A line of shorthand is on its way to Exeter in the margin of a letter.
Three letters are in Bistritz and on their way to Exeter.
Exeter has read your letters in his hand and found nothing amiss.
You found the line in the margin, and he does not remember writing it.
The sisters are sulking in the east wing. They have not forgotten.

8.title: The Hold of the Demeter
8.description: The Demeter is a Russian schooner out of Varna, with a captain, two mates, a cook and five hands, who have been told she carries silver sand and boxes of mould for a firm in Whitby. You lie in your own earth under the hatches, with the crew's feet over your head and the sea against the planks. The passage is long: the Bosphorus, the Dardanelles, the Mediterranean, Gibraltar, Biscay, the Channel and the North Sea. You will be hungry before it is done, and a ship is a small place to be hungry in.

options.label: Keep to the earth and ask nothing of the crew.
options.detail: Starve through the voyage. No man is touched, and none will talk. You arrive weak.

quote.speaker: Ship's mate
quote.text: There is something wrong with the hold, captain. The men say it smells of a church-yard. I say it is the earth.

options.outcome: You lie still for fourteen days. The crew grow uneasy about the boxes in the hold, as men do about things they have been told to leave alone, but none of them opens one. You arrive weak and unseen.

options.label: Take what you need from the crew, one at a time, at a rate nobody will count.
options.detail: Take one man at a time. A man lost overboard is a sailor's death, and sailors count them.

quote.speaker: Captain's log
quote.text: Things so strange happening, that I shall keep accurate note henceforth till we land.

options.outcome: By Biscay the watch has a man short, and the mate has taken to carrying a knife. By the Channel there are only the captain and the mate. You do not enjoy it. You do it all the same, and later you will call it necessary.

options.label: Work the weather: call the fog and the following wind, and make the passage in half the time.
options.detail: Call fog and wind to halve the voyage. It is hard work, and the crew will feel the weather turn.

quote.speaker: Captain's log
quote.text: A wind came up from nowhere and has not dropped for three days. The men say it is a miracle. I say I have never seen the like.

success.outcome: A fog comes up behind the ship and a wind pushes her through it. In seven days she makes what would have taken fourteen. The crew sleep soundly and do not remember dreaming, and you need take nothing from them. You are tired when you reach the Channel.

failure.outcome: The wind answers, and then does not stop. For two nights the schooner runs before a gale that you cannot turn. The mate is sure it is the box. He is not wrong. You will pay for the effort in a long hunger, and in the way the crew look at the hatch.

echoes.text: Fifty boxes lie in the hold over your head.

9.title: The Last Night at Sea
9.description: The Yorkshire coast comes up out of the fog on the last night, a black line with a few lights. Ahead is Whitby: a harbour, a pier, a town on both sides of a river, and above it a ruined abbey and a churchyard on the cliff. A storm is making in the east. In the next few hours a ship will come in, with or without a crew, and fifty boxes, or forty, or twenty, will need to be landed and carried to a house you have never seen. You have to decide in what shape to arrive.

options.label: Leave the ship in the shape of a great dog, and let the boxes be landed by the book.
options.detail: As a dog you can cross the whole harbour unremarked. The boxes go ashore under the paper.

quote.speaker: Coastguard
quote.text: A great dog, miss, as big as a calf. It went over the side and up the steps like a bat out of hell.

options.outcome: As the schooner grinds onto the sand below the churchyard you go over the bow and up the Abbey steps, grey and low and very fast. A crowd watches the ship. Nobody watches the dog.

options.label: Land the boxes quietly in the dark, through Billington and Son, and be on the first train south.
options.detail: Billington and Son take the cargo off the quay by paper. It is dull, and it is safe.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: A consignment of boxes of mould for a Count Dracula, at Carfax. We shall see it to the Great Northern tomorrow.

options.outcome: Billington and Son have the bill of lading, the carter and the railway van arranged before the ship is made fast. A clerk with a lantern signs for fifty boxes and does not look into one. You are on the night train south before the town knows what has come ashore.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE LAW

options.label: Run the ship in under full sail through the storm, and go ashore in the confusion.
options.detail: Wreck her on the sand and walk ashore in the crowd. The hold may break open.

quote.speaker: Whitby harbour-master
quote.text: She came in under full canvas with nobody at the wheel. I have been thirty years on this coast and I never saw the like.

success.outcome: The schooner drives onto the sand below the churchyard and holds. The crowd comes down the cliff path with lanterns. You are one more shadow among them, and then you are not there at all.

failure.outcome: A sea takes the schooner on the quarter and rolls her onto her side on the rocks. The hold breaks open. Boxes of earth are floating in the surf, and the crowd is running down the steps to pick them up.

echoes.text: The crew are fewer than they were, and the mate sleeps with a knife.
The crew are alive, and uneasy about the hold.
The fog you called rides at the stern, and is faithful.
The gale you raised did not stop when you wished it to.

10.title: The Seat on the East Cliff
10.description: The churchyard of St Mary's stands on the cliff above the town, with a bench over a suicide's grave looking out to sea. The old man who sits there every evening has watched you twice and has begun to nod. Two young women walk up most evenings and sit on the next bench: one dark, one fair. The fair one, Lucy, walks in her sleep and is to be married. The dark one, Mina, writes in a notebook in a script that only she can read. She is to marry the man you left in the castle.

options.label: Pass them all by, and keep to the dark.
options.detail: You came to England to settle, not to hunt in the first week.

quote.speaker: Old Mr Swales
quote.text: There is a thing that goes through this churchyard at night, miss, and I do not mean the dead.

options.outcome: You keep the Abbey wall between you and the bench and let them talk. The old man looks round once and sees nothing. Within the week you are in a railway van, and Whitby has become a place where you were never noticed.

options.label: The fair girl: she walks in her sleep, and her window looks over the steps.
options.detail: Lucy sleepwalks to her window above the steps. The old man on the bench may be watching.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: I do not know why I walked out. I only know I woke on the seat and I was very cold, and very happy.

success.outcome: For three nights you visit her window and the fair head turns on the pillow. By the fourth she walks out in her nightdress to meet you and you sit on the bench together in the dark. She wakes at dawn with two small marks at her throat and a dream she will not tell her friend.

failure.outcome: She is awake when you reach the window, and she is not alone: an old man on the Abbey wall is watching the steps. She draws the curtain. When you turn from the glass he is standing very still, with his stick.

options.label: The dark one with the notebook: she is engaged to the man in your north room.
options.detail: Mina writes everything down. Learn what she knows before she learns it of you.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I sat on the seat and wrote down the whole of the storm. I should have liked to know who the tall gentleman was who stood by the abbey wall.

options.outcome: You stand under the Abbey wall in the dusk and watch her write. She looks up once, straight at you, and does not look away. For a moment you are afraid. Then she turns back to her book.

echoes.text: A grey dog has been seen on the Abbey steps. The town has already begun to improve the story.
The Demeter is on the sand, and the whole of Whitby is on the cliff to look at her.
The harbour clerk has your name in a book. It is a very proper book.
Every dog in Whitby went down to the beach last night. People are talking about it.

11.title: Carfax
11.description: Carfax stands at the edge of Purfleet behind a wall, an old stone house with a chapel at the back. On the far side of the wall are the lit windows of a private asylum. Carter, Paterson and Company's carts bring your boxes up the drive, one after another, and a man in a leather apron signs for them. In the asylum next door a patient lifts his head at his window the moment you walk through the gate. You feel him before you see him: a small, hungry mind. You have a house in England and a month to decide what you are going to be in it.

options.label: Be a neighbour: take the house quietly, buy a second, disturb nothing, and let London forget you.
options.detail: Quiet and slow. London has millions of people, and takes years to notice one more.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: Count Dracula is the quietest tenant we have ever had, sir. One might almost say he is not there.

options.outcome: You take a second house through Billington and Son. You buy the right kinds of newspaper. You walk in your own garden at night and draw no attention. The city is vast and has plenty else to look at.

options.label: Be a host: take a place in society and make the people you need glad to know you.
options.detail: Cards, a box for the Season, a manner. Men who are invited are rarely searched.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: A foreign nobleman of the very first rank, sir, and a perfect gentleman. He asks after everyone.

options.outcome: You have your cards printed. You hire a box for the Season. You let it be known, discreetly, that the new owner of Carfax is a gentleman of ancient family who is in need of society. The invitations arrive within the week.

options.label: Be a storm: you did not come to England to be polite.
options.detail: Four centuries of waiting. Hunt freely, put fear into the city, and see what it does.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: The Master is coming. The Master has come. The Master will have all the flies.

options.outcome: You put on your oldest face. You go out on the third night with the fog behind you and a grey wolf at your heel. The first constable who sees you will not describe what he saw.

options.label: First, find out who is next door.
options.detail: The mind at the asylum window. It seems to know you already.

quote.speaker: You
quote.text: A mind like a hungry dog. It has been waiting for someone for a very long time.

options.outcome: You stand in the shrubbery at the end of the garden and let your attention reach over the wall. There is a man in a white room with a box of flies on his knee. He is quite mad. He is also, you find, quite certain of who you are.

echoes.text: You count the boxes as they come off the carts. There are twelve fewer than you wanted.
Ten boxes lie in the castle crypt behind a locked door. It is a long way from here.
Twenty boxes is a small household. It will be a very easy house to move.
The boxes you lost are counted in a book at Whitby.
You passed through Whitby unnoticed, which is a thing of some value.
The Minster at York is in your memory, shut and silent.
The town's favourite story is about a tall man in the churchyard, and nobody believes it.
The old man on the bench is dead, and the coastguard took his cap off.
You left Whitby on the milk train, and your face is forgotten.
An old man on the Abbey wall saw you take a girl's hand.

9-X.title: Boxes in the Surf
9-X.description: By morning half the town is on the sand. A coastguard in oilskins is counting the boxes that came ashore, and a clerk from the harbour office is writing the count in a book. Several of the chests have broken open. Earth from the other side of Europe lies in the shingle, and a boy picks up a handful and smells it. You are in the churchyard on the cliff in the shape of a man in a dark coat, and you have perhaps two hours before the sun comes over the sea.

options.label: Go down at dusk with a cart, claim the boxes as your own, and pay for the damage.
options.detail: Claim the boxes as the consignee, through Billington and Son, and pay the harbour dues.

quote.speaker: Harbour clerk
quote.text: A Count Dracula, sir? We have the bill of lading. I am sorry, sir, for your loss.

options.outcome: The clerk has the paper and the carter has the cart. The boxes are counted again and signed for, and you are driven away in a hired fly with the earth under a tarpaulin. It is humiliating, and it works.

options.label: Call the dogs of the town to the beach, and have the crowd driven off for a night.
options.detail: The dogs will drive the crowd off for a night. The town will remember it.

quote.speaker: Coastguard
quote.text: I never saw a dog behave so. Every cur in Whitby in the surf, and not a one of them barking.

options.outcome: Every dog in Whitby goes down to the beach in the dark and stands in a ring round the boxes. The coastguard withdraws. By the time he returns with a lantern, the boxes have gone, and so have the dogs.

options.label: Leave twelve of them where they lie and save the rest in the dark.
options.detail: Twelve boxes are left to the tide, and you will be twelve beds short in London.

quote.speaker: Harbour clerk
quote.text: Twelve are missing from the count, sir, but the sea takes what it likes.

options.outcome: You work all night with a cart you have borrowed, and you have saved what you can. Twelve of the chests stay on the sand to be dug over by children. You will be twelve beds short in London.

10-QUIET.title: The Night Train South
10-QUIET.description: The luggage van smells of fish and coal. Your boxes are stacked against the wall under a tarpaulin and a Great Northern porter, who has been given a sovereign by Billington and Son, has not looked at them. The train runs south through the dark, through York and Doncaster and Peterborough. You have never travelled so fast, and you are, at last, in the country you have spent half a year reading. It is smaller than the books suggest, and better lit.

options.label: Ride in the luggage van with the boxes, in the dark.
options.detail: The boxes, the dark, your own earth under you. You rest and see nothing of England.

quote.speaker: Porter
quote.text: A lot of boxes, sir. I never saw such a lot of boxes. Heavy, too.

options.outcome: You lie in the van among the boxes and the train carries you south. You rest, though you do not sleep. At King's Cross the van is shunted, and no one has seen you.

options.label: Take a first-class compartment as a foreign gentleman and read the newspaper.
options.detail: Dress, read the papers and be seen by a conductor. You learn how an Englishman travels.

quote.speaker: Guard
quote.text: First-class to King's Cross, sir. We have an hour at Peterborough. Will you take tea?

options.outcome: You read the Dailygraph and the Times, and are asked at Peterborough whether you will take tea. You say that you will not, but thank him for the thought. He remembers you as a very correct gentleman. He will not remember much else.

options.label: Get down at York and walk the city for an hour before the train goes on.
options.detail: There is a cathedral in York. You have not been in one for a long time.

quote.speaker: Cab-driver
quote.text: York Minster, sir? At this hour? It is shut, sir. Everything is shut.

options.outcome: You walk in the lee of the Minster for an hour. The doors are locked and the bells are silent. Nothing is asked of you. You have never seen a city so quiet, and you board the next train as if you had left something behind.

11-ASYLUM.title: The Patient Next Door
11-ASYLUM.description: His name is Renfield, and he is fifty-nine years old, and he eats flies. He has a theory, which he has had for a long time, that life is to be gained by taking it: first flies, then spiders to eat the flies, then sparrows to eat the spiders, then a cat. He has great patience and no morals whatever. He has felt you at the gate. He says, in his white room, aloud, that the Master is come and that the Master will reward his faithful servants with many lives. He is entirely sincere.

options.label: Offer him what he wants: lives, small and many, if he will watch the house.
options.detail: Renfield will watch the lane and report. He will want paying in lives, and he will be hard to keep quiet.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: I am here to do your bidding, Master. I am your slave, and you will reward me, for I shall be faithful.

options.outcome: You tell him through the wall that if he is faithful he will have lives. You tell him which ones: sparrows first, then others. He weeps, and promises, and a little of Renfield's will leaks into your own. You have a servant.

options.label: Answer him with nothing, and let him rave.
options.detail: Ignore him. The more he raves, the less Dr Seward credits it, and the more Seward writes down.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: My patient is much agitated tonight. He says the Master has arrived. I find myself wishing I knew what he meant.

options.outcome: You turn from the wall and walk away. The man in the white room goes on shouting at the dark. Dr Seward writes it all down in his case-book, carefully, in the morning.

options.label: Tell him the Master is not coming. Let him think he has been mistaken.
options.detail: Tell him he was wrong. He will stop watching, and he may stop believing in you.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: No Master? No lives? Then why did I hear him? Why did I feel the cold at the gate?

options.outcome: He is very disappointed. He weeps for an hour and then falls silent. Dr Seward notes the change in the morning with surprise and some relief. You have a neighbour who has stopped expecting you, and you are not sure that this was wise.

11-PLAN.title: Three Ways to Take a City
11-PLAN.description: You sit in the study at Carfax with the lamp turned low and the map of London on the table. The boxes are in the chapel. The deed is in the strong-room. There are the books, the money, the long nights and the whole of an enormous city to learn. You have come a long way in miles and a longer way in years. It is time to decide, once, how to be here.

options.label: Be a neighbour: take the house quietly, buy a second, disturb nothing, and let London forget you.
options.detail: Quiet and slow. London has millions of people, and takes years to notice one more.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: Count Dracula is the quietest tenant we have ever had, sir. One might almost say he is not there.

options.outcome: You take a second house through Billington and Son. You buy the right kinds of newspaper. You walk in your own garden at night and draw no attention. The city is vast and has plenty else to look at.

options.label: Be a host: take a place in society and make the people you need glad to know you.
options.detail: Cards, a box for the Season, a manner. Men who are invited are rarely searched.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: A foreign nobleman of the very first rank, sir, and a perfect gentleman. He asks after everyone.

options.outcome: You have your cards printed. You hire a box for the Season. You let it be known, discreetly, that the new owner of Carfax is a gentleman of ancient family who is in need of society. The invitations arrive within the week.

options.label: Be a storm: you did not come to England to be polite.
options.detail: Four centuries of waiting. Hunt freely, put fear into the city, and see what it does.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: The Master is coming. The Master has come. The Master will have all the flies.

options.outcome: You put on your oldest face. You go out on the third night with the fog behind you and a grey wolf at your heel. The first constable who sees you will not describe what he saw.

echoes.text: Next door a man is watching the road for you. He has been told he will be rewarded.
Next door a man is shouting that the Master has come. A doctor is listening.
Next door a man has gone silent. A doctor has noticed that too.

12A.title: A Second House
12A.description: Carfax is a good house and a known one. The boxes can rest there, but a prudent man keeps a second door. A firm of house agents has shown you a tall house in Piccadilly with its blinds down and a cellar that has been dry since the Regency. They have also shown you a lodging-house yard at Mile End, which is cheaper and not much of a residence. You can have either by the end of the month. You can have both if you are willing to be seen paying for them.

options.label: Buy Piccadilly by the book: survey, searches, a solicitor's letter, and a lease no one reads.
options.detail: Slow and legal. Piccadilly is yours in a fortnight, on paper that raises no question.

quote.speaker: House agent
quote.text: The title is perfectly clear, Count. I do not think any one will ever ask a question about it.

options.outcome: The agents do it properly. The searches are made, the survey is signed, and the deed goes into the strong-room at Carfax with a small stain on one corner. The house in Piccadilly is yours in a fortnight, and the street does not know who bought it.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE LAW

options.label: Pay in banknotes over the counter, and be in by the end of the week.
options.detail: Fast and traceable. A clerk who takes your notes will be remembered.

quote.speaker: Clerk
quote.text: I have not seen your face, sir. I have not seen a thing. The house is entirely yours.

options.outcome: The clerk has a wife in Camberwell and a brother who needs a position. You take possession on Friday, after the street lamps are lit. There is a note of the transaction somewhere, in a drawer, that has no reason to be read.

options.label: Skip the purchase. Rent cellars in the East End by the quarter, in three names.
options.detail: Three damp cellars in three names. Nothing in them to trace.

quote.speaker: Landlord
quote.text: Three cellars, three names, three quarters in advance. I am not asking, sir. Nobody asks in Mile End.

options.outcome: You take three cellars from three landlords in three names, each of them a damp brick room that has not seen the sun in twenty years. They are not places a man would choose to live. They are good places to be lost.

13A.title: The Neighbour in the White Coat
13A.description: Dr John Seward keeps the asylum at Purfleet. He is a young man, thorough, kindly and tired. He dictates his case-notes every evening into a phonograph, and he has taken an interest in his patient Renfield. He has also begun, with great courtesy, to take an interest in the new owner of Carfax. He has noticed that no lights are lit at the house after dark. He has written down that a bell rang in the chapel last Tuesday, though the bell was taken out a hundred years ago.

options.label: Keep Renfield sweet with small mercies, and he will tell Seward nothing.
options.detail: Renfield is kept calm with promises. Seward sees an improvement and wonders why.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: Renfield has been calmer this week, which I find more disquieting than his raving. He says the Master is satisfied.

options.outcome: You send a thought across the wall at dusk, and receive a flicker of joy. For a week Renfield is a model patient. He eats his flies and keeps his counsel. Dr Seward records an improvement, and begins to wonder about it.

options.label: Put out every light at Carfax and keep the chapel door shut: be a house nobody has seen.
options.detail: No lamps, no fires, the chapel shut. From the road, Carfax is an empty house.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: I have looked at Carfax from my study window every night for a fortnight. It has not shown a light. I cannot decide whether it is empty or very well kept.

options.outcome: You live by feel, and by the smell of old earth. The house has no lamps and no fires. A policeman on his round at Purfleet tests the gate, finds it locked, and passes on. From the road, Carfax is an empty house.

options.label: Call on Dr Seward as a foreign gentleman, in the late afternoon, in a fog.
options.detail: A call at the end of the afternoon, in a fog. Seward notices things, and he will notice you.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: A most courteous gentleman. He asked about the drainage of the property, and whether the wall was sound. I find I rather like him.

success.outcome: The fog is on your side and so is your English. Dr Seward gives you tea, shows you the garden, and does not once ask you what you do at night. By the time you leave he is sure he has made a friend. He says so in the phonograph that evening.

failure.outcome: You are shown into the study at a bad moment. The doctor looks at your hands, at your feet and at the window behind you, which has no reflection in the glass. He is polite. He sees you to the gate himself. He writes for an hour that night, and does not dictate it.

options.label: Dine with Dr Seward, as a foreign gentleman who knows how an Englishman dines.
options.detail: Eat a proper English dinner with him. It costs you an evening of pretending.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: I do not know when I have had so agreeable an evening. He knows a good deal about the world, and a great deal about asylums.

options.outcome: You dine in Dr Seward's study on a joint and a pudding and an ordinary claret, and you eat a little of each in the proper order. He talks about his patient. You talk about the drains. He sees you to the gate himself and hopes that you will call again.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF MANNERS

14A.title: A Sleeping Girl at Hillingham
14A.description: Lucy Westenra lives at Hillingham, on the edge of Hampstead, with a mother whose heart is weak and a doctor's attention that is not. She is young, and has been unwell, and sleeps by an open window. She is a short night's journey from Carfax. A quiet colony does not need a girl in Hampstead. It needs only to be left alone, and it has never been so quiet.

options.label: Leave her alone. She will mend, and the doctors will be satisfied.
options.detail: Do not feed. You grow thin and slow, and she recovers.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: I slept so well last night. I do not know why I ever worried. There was nothing at the window at all.

options.outcome: You keep to your own side of the wall. You eat very little. A week on, you are lean and slow, and Lucy Westenra is sleeping through the night. You do not know whether you have done right. You are sure only that you have done no harm.

options.label: Visit once, take what you need, and stop.
options.detail: One visit, one small feeding. She will think she had a bad night.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: I dreamed a tall man bent over me, and I was not frightened. I woke with a headache and a little mark at my throat.

options.outcome: She does not wake. You take no more than you need and you close the window behind you. In the morning she is pale and her mother thinks it is the heat. A doctor is sent for, and tells her to rest.

options.label: Visit her through the autumn, patiently, until she is yours.
options.detail: Visit her through the autumn. She grows paler, and her mother and her doctors will notice.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: I cannot understand it. She loses colour daily and I can find nothing wrong with her. I have sent for my old master in Amsterdam.

options.outcome: You come to the window on seven nights. Each time she is a little paler and a little more yours. Her mother notices, her doctor notices and, at last, so do her suitors. Within the month there is a man in the house with a bag of instruments, asking about the window.

echoes.text: You marked her at Whitby, on the bench, and she has not forgotten you.
Her friend, the dark one with the notebook, writes to her from Exeter every day. You can see the postmarks from the street.
Renfield is quiet. The doctor is making notes.
Carfax has no light at all. A policeman tries the gate every night.
Dr Seward has dined with you, and thinks you the most agreeable of neighbours.

15A.title: The Doctor from Amsterdam
15A.description: Dr Seward has written to his old master in Amsterdam, a physician and philosopher named Abraham Van Helsing. The old man arrives by the evening boat-train with two bags and a small leather case. He examines the girl, or the patient, with an attention you have not met in a doctor for several centuries. Then he asks the household for garlic, and they bring it, because he asks quietly and does not explain. He is not a man who is surprised by things. He is looking, with great patience, for you.

options.label: Come to him in a dream, and learn how much he knows.
options.detail: Enter his sleep and read what he knows. If he wakes, he will know you were there.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: I dreamed a tall man stood at the foot of my bed, and in the morning I had the whole of his face. Seward says it is the journey.

success.outcome: The old man dreams and you step into the dream as into a room. He knows about Whitby. He knows about the Demeter. He knows that you can be turned back by a cross and a flower, and has not yet decided to believe it. You wake knowing his plan, and he wakes knowing nothing.

failure.outcome: The old man dreams of a tall man at the foot of his bed. He wakes at once, and does not turn on a light. He takes down a crucifix from his bag and hangs it on the bedpost. You are shut out of the dream like a door.

options.label: Keep your wolves from Seward's gate, and your own face from the windows. Let the old man find nothing.
options.detail: Keep every animal and every light away from Seward's gate. He finds nothing to hunt.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Nothing, Seward. There is nothing at all. That is what troubles me. There is a great deal of nothing in this garden.

options.outcome: You do not go out. The wolves are sent to the hills, the rats are sent to the cellars, and the fog is asked to stay in the river. The old man walks the grounds at night and finds an empty house with no light in it. He does not believe it.

options.label: Meet him as a stranger in a bookshop, a scholar of Transylvanian antiquities.
options.detail: Talk to him as a scholar, truthfully. He will like you, and be slow to suspect you.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A delightful man. We spoke for an hour about the Voivodes, and he knew a great deal about their customs. I wish I could remember his name.

options.outcome: The old man is in a bookshop in Charing Cross Road on a wet afternoon, looking for a seventeenth-century herbal. You talk for an hour. He is delighted. He tells you a number of things he has not told anyone, and you tell him a number of things that are quite true. He leaves without noticing that you have not given him your card.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF DOCTORS

echoes.text: Dr Seward has already written to Van Helsing about the man at Carfax.
Dr Seward thinks well of you, which is why the old man has been so careful to ask about you.
The girl at Hampstead is sleeping through the night.
The old man is at Hillingham already, asking about the window.
You took a little from the girl at Hampstead, once, and she thinks she was ill.

15A-X.title: The Cross at the Pillow
15A-X.description: You are in the earth at Carfax with the lid pulled down, and you cannot sleep. Something in the old man's mind has turned you out like a dog from a church. In the house at Hampstead he has hung a cross at the head of his bed and a wreath of white flowers on the window, and the air in the room smells of garlic. You can feel it from across the river. A day of sleep has been lost, and a night of hunting, and the old man now knows exactly what he is looking for.

options.label: Retreat into the earth and give him a week's quiet.
options.detail: He has seen you once in a dream. He will not see you again if you do not come.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He has gone to ground, Seward. A thing of that sort does when it is frightened, and I would rather he were angry.

options.outcome: You lie in your box and keep your mind shut. For a week the old man hunts nothing, and begins to doubt himself. He sends for his friends all the same.

options.label: Answer him the next night, at his window, and let him see what he has been dreaming of.
options.detail: Show yourself at his window. He will know exactly what he faces.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: He says there was a man at the window, Arthur. He says the window is on the second floor. He is quite calm about it.

options.outcome: You come to the window of the room where he sleeps, as a grey mist against the glass. He sits up. He does not cry out. The crucifix on his bed shows a faint light, and you go away.

options.label: Send the rats to the old man's room and the wolf to the garden gate.
options.detail: Rats in his room, a wolf at his gate. It will tire him, and tell him nothing new.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: The professor says there were rats in the walls all night. I had the house inspected in the afternoon. It is perfectly sound.

options.outcome: The rats go in by the thousand and the wolf sits at the gate. The old man does not sleep. In the morning he looks ten years older, and he has made a list.

16A.title: The Boxes at Carfax
16A.description: They come by day, five men with a locksmith and a lantern, and a young woman with a typewriter waiting at the gate. Lord Godalming opens the door because it is his right to open any door. They find the chapel and the boxes in the chapel, and the old man kneels in the dust of the nave with a silver case and lays a fragment of white bread in every chest. You know it the moment it begins. In the cellars across the city, you feel each of the beds go dead like a tooth, one after another.

options.label: Move what you can to the other house the night before, each box a lair saved.
options.detail: Move boxes to the second house in one night. You cannot save them all.

quote.speaker: Carter
quote.text: Eleven boxes in one night, sir, and not a word. I do not like it. I will do it for the money.

success.outcome: You work through the night with a hired cart and two men who are paid not to wonder. By dawn eleven boxes have been moved and the rest are left for the hunters. It is a poor trade, but you have saved eleven beds out of twenty-nine.

failure.outcome: The cart is late and the dawn is early. You get four boxes into the cellar before the sky greys, and you finish the night in a coal-hole with your hand over your eyes. Seven boxes are left in the chapel for the old man.

options.label: Let Carfax go. You have other places.
options.detail: Give up the chapel boxes and keep your strength.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: They are sealed, my friends, every one. We have closed a door in his house. There are others, and we shall find them.

options.outcome: You watch from the roof of a house a mile away as the hunters leave Carfax in the dusk. Twenty-nine boxes are dead and you feel each one. It is a lot to lose in an afternoon, and you do not intend to lose any more.

options.label: Wait in the dark and take the first man through the door.
options.detail: Wait in the crypt. One of them will go down alone.

quote.speaker: Locksmith
quote.text: Something took hold of me in the dark, gentlemen. I do not know what. I have never been so frightened.

success.outcome: The locksmith goes down to the crypt alone to see about a rusty hinge. He does not call out, and he is sitting on the stairs when they find him, quite pale. They know that something has been in the cellar. They are right.

failure.outcome: There is a lantern at the foot of the stairs, and the man holding it has been waiting for you.

echoes.text: You know the old man's plan, and he does not know you do.
The old man woke in his dream, and has been wary since.
You have not left the house for a week. The old man is puzzled.
The old man liked you, and does not know why that troubles him.
You have kept still for a week, and so has the old man.
The old man has seen your face at his window.
The old man sits up with rats in the walls, and is tired.

17A.title: Mrs Harker
17A.description: One of the hunters is a young woman. She has married Jonathan Harker, who came home from the Carpathians with white hair, and she has typed his journal, Dr Seward's phonograph cylinders and her own diary into a single set of papers that every one of the hunters reads. She has, in a way that London's police have never managed, put together what you are. She knows the boxes, the houses, the Demeter's log, and a good deal about your hours. She is the cleverest of them. In the quiet colony she is the one who will find you, or the one you might take.

options.label: Leave the Harkers alone. Their quarrel is not with you.
options.detail: Stay away from the Harkers and from Purfleet. Your quarrel with them goes quiet.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I shall type it once more, Jonathan, and then I shall put it in a locked drawer. I do not think it will be needed.

options.outcome: You keep away from Purfleet and from the house where the Harkers are lodging. You are lean, and tired, and not at all a figure of terror. By the spring you are almost a man who has given something up.

options.label: Read what she has typed: go once to the room where she works, and learn how much they know.
options.detail: Read her papers while she sleeps. You will know what the hunters know.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I woke at two and the papers on the desk had been moved. I thought it was the draught, and I put them back.

options.outcome: You stand over her desk for an hour in the dark and read the whole of it. It is very good. It is more thorough than any account of yourself you could have written. When you leave she sleeps on, a little frowning, with her hand on the typewriter.

options.label: Take her. She is the cleverest of them, and she would be at your side.
options.detail: Take her, as you took Lucy. She will not forget it, and the hunters will come for her.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: Unclean, unclean! I must touch him or kiss him no more.

options.outcome: The window is shut and the room is cold. She is awake, and she does not scream; she looks at you as she would look at a fact she had been expecting. You do what you came to do. When the men break in with their candles and their bread you give her up, and go, and she will remember every minute.

echoes.text: Her husband never came home. She has typed what she could from his letters and the Demeter's log.
He walked out of the castle in the morning and went home. She has his journal, and she has read it.
He found the key in a day or two, and a rope in a week. She has his journal, and she has read it.
Carfax is sealed, and you feel each of its beds as a dead tooth.
Eleven beds are safe in another cellar.
A locksmith sat on a stair and could not say what had happened to him.
Only four beds got out of Carfax, and seven are left for the old man.
You gave them an empty crypt and lay in the wall for an hour.
The rats put out the lantern, and a young man dropped his cross.
You stared down a young man with a cross, and it cost you.

18A.title: The Last Lair
18A.description: Carfax is sealed. The hunters have found Piccadilly, or are about to, and the list of your lairs is a shorter list than it was. At Lloyd's, a steamer called the Czarina Catherine is advertised for Varna on the next tide. In London the autumn is turning cold, and the fog is no longer your servant but a thing that you cannot see through. You are much lighter than you were. What remains is a short list of ways to be alive.

options.label: Book a berth in the Czarina Catherine, with the one box you can still reach.
options.detail: A single box and a ship's hold. You know the sea, and you know the road at the end of it.

quote.speaker: Lloyd's agent
quote.text: A single large box for a forwarding agent at Galatz. Our master has no passengers, sir. It will go with the freight.

options.outcome: A single box is a small cargo. You arrange it with a forwarding agent, and a carter who asks nothing, and a captain who has been told that the chest is a collection of Transylvanian mould for a museum.

options.label: Stay. There is a cellar nobody knows.
options.detail: Wait in an East End cellar the hunters have not found. It is cheap, and they are drawing closer.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is still in London, my friends. I can feel it. He has gone to ground like a fox in a drain.

options.outcome: You settle in one of the East End cellars with a box and a candle that you do not light. The city goes on overhead. You can hear the carts, the church bells and the cries of a street where your name means nothing. You have waited in worse.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS A SECOND PLACE THE HUNTERS HAVE NOT FOUND

options.label: Go to ground in the city: change cellars every night, and trust the fog.
options.detail: Move cellar every night. It is hard on you, and harder to find you.

quote.speaker: Cab-driver
quote.text: I picked up a foreign gentleman in Camden Town, and I put him down in Bermondsey. I never saw a man so grey.

options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE CITY

success.outcome: You walk the streets every night from cellar to cellar, with your box carried ahead of you in a cart by men who forget your face as soon as they have been paid. You are never in the same place for two days. You have never been so tired.

failure.outcome: A constable stops the cart at the end of Jamaica Lane and asks what is in the box. You answer for the carter, and he lets you go, and he remembers.

echoes.text: You stayed away from Purfleet, and the typewriter did not stop.
You have read the whole of her account, and you know what they know.

19A.title: Three Roads Out of London
19A.description: The year has turned. The hunters have sealed every house they know, and some they do not, and the list in the old man's notebook is almost a list of the places you are. London is cold and wet and large. There are three roads out of this: a ship, a cellar or the sun. Whichever you take, it is the last decision you will make in England.

options.label: Stay in London, in the last house they have not found, and wait for the hunt to tire.
options.detail: Lie low through the winter. The old man will tire, or he will not.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: We shall never find him, Jonathan. I begin to think he has simply stopped. It is very odd to be sorry.

options.outcome: You take the last cellar, the one in Mile End that no list names. The carter is paid and forgotten, the candle stays unlit, and for the first time in weeks you are not hurried.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS THE HUNTERS NOT TO KNOW WHERE YOU ARE

options.label: Take the Czarina Catherine home, with the one box you saved.
options.detail: The sea is the way you came. The hunters cannot watch a whole ship.

quote.speaker: Captain
quote.text: A single box of mould, for a museum, and no passengers. We shall be in Varna in ten days if the weather holds.

options.outcome: You pay the agent in notes, and the single box goes aboard at the Pool after dark, entered as mould for a museum. The captain has been told to keep his men from the hatch.

options.label: Go home as you came: by the road, in the light the hunters are counting on.
options.detail: The Slovaks will meet you. The road is open. It is the oldest way, and the only one you know by heart.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Mr Harker, you take the throat. I will see to the heart. Ma'am, you keep behind the Doc.

options.outcome: You send word to the Slovaks at Galatz and take the long way: rail to Varna, a wagon at the border, the box under sacking. The road is open, and you know every turn of it.

options.label: Close the door. Go home, and seal yourself in the crypt of the castle chapel, and sleep.
options.detail: Go home, seal the crypt and sleep. For the first time in your life, you are tired.

quote.speaker: You
quote.text: It has been a very long night. You would like, for once, to be somewhere nobody has a name for you.

options.outcome: You settle what can be settled: the deed to Billington's strong-room, the last bill paid, the box ordered to Dover. There is nothing else to leave behind.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS A HOME TO GO BACK TO, AND SOMETHING IN YOU THAT WANTS TO

echoes.text: You are in a cellar the hunters do not know, and the city goes on over your head.
You have not slept in the same place twice.
A constable at Jamaica Lane remembers a gentleman who answered for his carter.

12B.title: A Foreign Gentleman
12B.description: London in autumn is thin of society, but there are dinners, a few boxes at the opera, and two or three clubs that elect foreign noblemen for the sake of the novelty. You have a title, a house with a chapel, a second name for London, Count de Ville, which nobody has yet had time to dislike, an accent that Harker corrected until it was nearly flawless, and an unlimited quantity of old gold. What you do not have is anyone who will vouch for you. A nobleman without friends is a curiosity. A nobleman with three friends is a gentleman.

options.label: Take a box at the opera and let the Season find you.
options.detail: A box at the opera. Be seen, listen, eat nothing. One slip would be remembered.

quote.speaker: Lady at the opera
quote.text: A Count from the Carpathians, my dear, and unmarried. He sat through the whole of the third act without once looking at the stage.

options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF MANNERS

success.outcome: You take a box for the Season, in the second tier, and you do not eat the supper. By the third week your name is on a list of three hundred and you are asked to dinner in Belgrave Square. People like a man who listens.

failure.outcome: The third act has hardly begun when somebody in the next box catches sight of you. You are not looking at the stage. You are looking at the throat of the lady in front. You turn your head, and you smile, and it is too late. The dinner invitations come all the same, but the people who send them have begun to talk.

options.label: Cultivate a solicitor, a banker and a doctor, one at a time, over dinner.
options.detail: A solicitor, a banker and a doctor, one dinner each. It takes patience.

quote.speaker: Banker
quote.text: A most agreeable foreign gentleman. He asks very sensible questions, and he never accepts a second glass.

options.outcome: You dine with each in turn at a good club, and you listen. Within the month you have a solicitor who will write a letter, a banker who will honour a draft and a doctor who will certify that you are in excellent health. You eat nothing at any of the dinners and the waiters do not remark on it.

options.label: Let it be known only that Carfax is let to a foreign nobleman, and wait to be asked.
options.detail: Stay at home and be talked about. The curious will come, and you choose which.

quote.speaker: Housemaid
quote.text: They say the gentleman at Carfax is a great lord, Mary, and never has a light on. He has the carts come in the dead of night.

options.outcome: You do not go out. The neighbours say that the foreign gentleman at Carfax is shy, and a great lord, and probably in mourning. The first invitation comes in a week, from a lady who is too curious to wait.

13B.title: A Faithful Servant
13B.description: The patient in the asylum next door has the one thing you cannot buy in England: an unreasoning devotion to a master he has never seen. He sits at his window, watches your road, and keeps his own record, in his own way, of everything that passes. He is a madman and a nuisance and a good servant. A court needs servants. It also needs to keep them quiet, and a servant who has been promised lives is not the quietest sort.

options.label: Make Renfield your steward in the asylum: tell him what to watch, and promise him lives.
options.detail: Renfield watches Seward and reports nightly. He will expect the lives you promised.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: I shall watch the gate, Master, and the road, and the doctor's study. I shall be the very best of servants.

options.outcome: You send him word across the wall of what he is to watch for and what he will get for it. He promises, and weeps, and promises again. For a week he is a model patient and every night he reports, in his own incoherent way, on Dr Seward.

options.label: Use him once, to open a door, and then leave him alone.
options.detail: One errand: a door left open at Hillingham. No standing orders.

quote.speaker: Renfield
quote.text: I opened the door, Master. I opened it quite quietly. Can I have a bird now?

options.outcome: He is let out of the asylum for one night by a door that someone has forgotten to lock. He opens a gate at Hillingham and is back in his bed before dawn. In the morning he asks for a sparrow.

options.label: Refuse him. A court has no place for a madman.
options.detail: Ignore his calls. He will wait, and may stop.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: Renfield has gone very quiet. He sits at his window and says nothing. I wonder what has been taken from him.

options.outcome: You do not answer his call. He waits at the window every night for a week and then, one night, he is not there. When Dr Seward looks into his room he is lying on the floor, wide awake, looking at the ceiling.

echoes.text: He has been waiting for you since the first night, and he cannot be put off.
He was ignored on the first night, and has not forgotten it.
You told him the Master was not coming, and he has been drawing pictures of you ever since.
A box at the opera, and three hundred names on a list.
A solicitor, a banker and a doctor think well of you.
The first invitation came from a lady who was too curious to wait.
A lady in the next box has told two friends what she thinks of a man who does not look at the stage.
A lady on your left has decided that you are a charming eccentric.
You have the taste of a Belgrave Square sole in your mouth, and it will not go.
Belgrave Square has decided that the foreign gentleman is delicate.

14B.title: The Fair Girl
14B.description: Lucy Westenra lives at Hillingham with a mother whose heart is weak and three men who have each asked to marry her. She is to marry one of them, and she is ill. A doctor has been called and a second doctor sent for. She is a girl who has been told to refuse everything she is offered. You could give her what none of them can. You could also take what none of them has noticed that she has.

options.label: Court her as a man courts: a letter, a visit by daylight, and then a visit by night. Let her come to you.
options.detail: Slow, and hers to refuse. She may say no, or tell a friend.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: I do not know why I want to see him, Mina. He is old and foreign and perfectly horrid. And I think I shall go on wanting to see him for ever.

success.outcome: You write to her under a name she thinks she has made up. You call in daylight, with a card. On the fourth night you stand at her window and she opens it herself. When she wakes in the morning she is pale and she smiles at her mother and says she has slept better than she has in a year.

failure.outcome: She is flattered and she is no fool. She puts your name in her diary with a question mark, and shows it to her friend, the dark one who writes everything down. You have been noticed by someone who keeps records.

options.label: Take her quickly. She is dying already of her doctors' ignorance.
options.detail: Four nights, quickly. She is weak, and the doctors will notice how weak.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: She is losing blood at a rate I cannot explain, and I can find no wound. I am quite out of my depth.

options.outcome: You come to the window on four nights in succession and take freely. She is a little paler each morning and a good deal more yours. The doctor writes to Amsterdam. Her mother begins to pray in the next room.

options.label: Leave her to her suitors and her doctors.
options.detail: Stay away. She mends, and Hillingham has no questions to ask.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: She is getting better, Seward. I cannot tell you how thankful I am. She slept through the night for the first time in a week.

options.outcome: You keep to your side of the city. The girl at Hillingham mends, or seems to, and her suitors send flowers. You are the only one who knows that it is not a miracle, and you do not like how little that helps.

options.label: Meet her family doctor first, and make him a friend.
options.detail: Befriend the doctor first. He will tell you the house's nights, and watch you less closely.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: A most agreeable foreign gentleman, and a very sound man on the subject of blood.

options.outcome: You call on him as a neighbour and a connoisseur of his profession. He is flattered. Over a glass of port he tells you which of Miss Westenra's suitors sits up with her, and on which nights. He tells you nothing else, because there is nothing else he knows.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF DOCTORS

echoes.text: You marked her at Whitby. She has been looking out of windows ever since.
You used Renfield once, and he has not stopped asking for a bird.
Renfield lies on the floor of his room, looking at the ceiling.

15B.title: The Professor's Garlic
15B.description: Dr Seward's old master has arrived from Amsterdam, and he has turned the girl's room into a church. There is a wreath of white flowers at the window, another at the door, a third round her neck. The window is bolted and the room is full of a smell like a crowded kitchen. You can feel it from across the city, like a hand pressed flat against your face. It is an old trick, and it works. Whatever you intend to do next in that house, you will have to do through somebody else.

options.label: Have the mother take down the flowers: she is old, anxious and easily moved.
options.detail: Work on her mother's mind. She will take the flowers down herself.

quote.speaker: Mrs Westenra
quote.text: The room smells like a drain, Lucy, and I will not have it. I shall take them away myself, and open the window for you.

options.outcome: You do not need to enter the room. You turn her thoughts in the night, as you might turn a key. In the morning she takes down the flowers with her own hands, opens the window and leaves her daughter asleep. She is kind. She does not remember why.

options.label: Send the wolf through the window: terror is a key.
options.detail: The wolf comes through the glass. The mother may not survive the fright.

quote.speaker: Zookeeper
quote.text: He was always the quietest wolf in the Gardens. I cannot account for it.

options.outcome: You tell the old grey wolf from the Gardens where to go. He goes through the glass at midnight, in a shower of splinters, and puts his front paws on the foot of the bed. The mother, who has been sitting up, makes a short sound and does not make another.

options.label: Stay away. The old man's flowers are strong. Let the girl be.
options.detail: Stay clear of the flowers. Let him sit up through his nights.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Nothing came last night. Nothing came the night before. I do not trust nothing, Seward.

options.outcome: You do not go. The flowers wither and are replaced. The old man sits up through the nights with a book in his lap, and in the day he walks the grounds and looks at the wall. You are beginning to find his patience more tiresome than his flowers.

options.label: Learn the hours of the house from the cabmen and the milkman, and come when nobody is awake.
options.detail: Learn the house from the cabman and the milkman. Slow, but no flowers can stop it.

quote.speaker: Cabman
quote.text: Half past two, sir, the house is as dead as a stone. The mother sits up till one, and she nods.

options.outcome: You buy a cabman a glass of beer and a milkman something stronger. In a week you know when the house is dark, which stair creaks, and where the dog sleeps.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE CITY

echoes.text: The girl is losing blood faster than the doctors can explain.
She asks about you in her sleep.
The girl at Hillingham is mending, and you do not take the credit.
She has put your name in her diary, with a question mark, and shown it to her friend.
Her doctor thinks well of you, and has told you which nights the house is watched.

16B.title: A Woman at a Typewriter
16B.description: In the house at Purfleet a young woman is typing. She is called Mina, she is the wife of a man who came home from the Carpathians with white hair, and she is putting together his journal, Dr Seward's cylinders and her own diary into a single account of you. She does it well. In a court of the marked and the faithful, she is the one thing you do not have: someone who sees you plainly. It is an attractive quality, to a man who is very old.

options.label: Come to her honestly, by night, and tell her what you are. Ask her to choose.
options.detail: Tell her what you are and ask her to choose. If she refuses, the house wakes.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I did not scream. I do not know why I did not scream. I sat up in bed with the candle and he stood at the foot of it and told me what he was.

success.outcome: She listens. She asks three questions, and they are the right ones, and you answer them truly. She says that she cannot say yes, and does not say no. She says she will think about it. You leave by the window with something that you cannot account for, and which you will carry for a long time.

failure.outcome: She is awake, with a candle and a crucifix on the desk, and she has been waiting for you. She looks at you and cries out, and the door is flung open and five men come in with their candles and their bread. You are a grey mist under the door before the first of them has crossed the room.

options.label: Take her in her bed, as you took the girl, and bind her to you.
options.detail: She is awake and clever. This ends in a bond or in a cry.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I woke with the taste of salt and iron in my mouth, and a man bending over me, and I could not call out.

options.outcome: The window is shut and the air is cold. She is awake and does not scream. You take what you came to take, and she keeps her eyes on yours until the end. When the door is broken in and the men come with their candles and their crosses and their bread, you give her up, and go.

options.label: Read her typed papers while she sleeps, and leave her alone.
options.detail: Read her account while she sleeps, and go. You learn what they know.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I woke at two and the papers on my desk had been moved. I thought it was a draught, and put them back.

options.outcome: You stand over her desk for an hour in the dark and read the whole of it. It is good. It is thorough, and it is very nearly fair. When you have finished you put the pages back in order, and she sleeps on, a little frowning, with her hand on the typewriter.

echoes.text: Her husband never came home. She is typing from the Demeter's log and a few letters, and she does not believe in them.
Lucy's mother is dead, and the house at Hillingham is in mourning. Mina spent three days there.
The wolf from the Gardens has been found and returned. The newspapers have been very amusing about it.
The old man's flowers wither and are replaced, every night.
You know when the house is dark, which stair creaks and where the dog sleeps.

16B-X.title: A Room Full of Garlic
16B-X.description: You are in the earth at Carfax with your mind going round and round the same point. She screamed because she had decided to, and that was worse than if she had been frightened. They have put garlic on the window and a cross on the pillow. Five men have heard what you said to her, and one of them is an old man with a notebook. You have lost a night, and you have lost something you did not know you had.

options.label: Retreat. Let a week go by and think again.
options.detail: Lie low for a week. She may not tell them all she knows.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I did not tell them what he said, Jonathan. I do not know why. It seemed like something that had been said to me.

options.outcome: You lie in your box for a week and think about it. In the evenings you go to the window of the house at Purfleet, and the light is on and a woman is typing.

options.label: Go back the next night and take her anyway.
options.detail: Past the cross and the garlic. It will hurt, and the old man will be waiting.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He came again, my friends. He came to her window, and the cross burned him. I have seen him. I know now what he is.

options.outcome: You come at the window on the second night, past the cross and the garlic, in the shape of a mist. The old man is waiting. The cross burns your hand, but you take her anyway, and you go with the taste of her in your mouth and a mark on your palm.

options.label: Send the wolf to the garden and the fog to the street, and watch her house from a distance.
options.detail: Fog in the lane and a wolf in the garden. Keep the house awake and afraid.

quote.speaker: Seward
quote.text: There is something in the fog. I cannot see it, but the horses will not go down the lane.

options.outcome: You send the fog down the lane like a long cold hand, and the horses will not pass. The hunters stay indoors. For three nights the house at Purfleet is a ship in a grey sea, and the people in it do not sleep.

17B.title: The Court Disperses
17B.description: The hunters have found the lairs. They go from house to house with their white bread and their locksmith, and every day there are fewer of your boxes and fewer of your people. A court is made of the things it holds and the people who agree to be held. One by one you can feel yours loosen. The girl at Hillingham is dead, or has changed. The patient in the asylum is silent. The woman at Purfleet is typing. You have a short night to decide what is worth keeping.

options.label: Break Renfield out of the asylum and keep him at Carfax.
options.detail: Free Renfield from the asylum. He will follow you anywhere and be hard to hide.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: He is gone. The window was open, and he is gone, and I do not understand how. The attendant says he heard nothing.
