options.outcome: You open a door in the asylum with a thought and he walks out into the night, barefoot, in his nightshirt. He is at Carfax before dawn, weeping and thanking you. He sleeps in the chapel on the floor.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS HIM BOUND TO YOU AS A SERVANT

options.label: Let the court go and keep only the house.
options.detail: Release your servants and keep the house. Less to defend, less to lose.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is deserted, my friends. Every one of his creatures has gone. It is a thing I have seen before. It is always the moment he is most dangerous.

options.outcome: You let every thread go. The servants you have marked, the butlers you have flattered, the friends you have made at dinner, all go quietly back to their own lives. You are left with a house, a few boxes, and the long night. It is quiet, and the quiet is almost a relief.

options.label: Hold a last night at Carfax and show every servant you have left who rules.
options.detail: Light every lamp and gather them. It is a show of strength, and the hunters will see it.

quote.speaker: Servant
quote.text: The master was never so splendid. We all stood in the hall and he looked at every one of us. I would die for him.

options.outcome: On the last night you light every lamp in Carfax for the first time. The servants, the friends, the creatures and the marked come into the hall, and you look at each of them. It is a fine hour. It is also a lot of light, and every window in Purfleet shows it.

options.label: Make Carfax yours in law: a deed of trust in Mr Billington's name, so that no one may enter without a warrant.
options.detail: Put Carfax in a trust. The hunters will need a magistrate before they can enter.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: A trust, Count? It is irregular, but perfectly sound. I do not think anyone will enter that house without a very good reason.

options.outcome: Billington and Son draw the deed in a week and sign it in your absence. The house at Purfleet now belongs to a trust of which you are the only beneficiary, and the only men who know of it are Billington and you. For a few days the hunters will have to find a magistrate.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE LAW

echoes.text: She screamed on purpose, and the whole house knows your face.
You have given her a week.
Your hand is marked by the cross, and will not heal quickly.
The fog is in the lane, and the horses will not come up it.

18B.title: The Last Night in London
18B.description: There are only a few nights left. The hunters have found Piccadilly and are working through the rest, and in the old man's notebook there is a list of your houses with most of them crossed through. London is cold and the Thames is high. The Czarina Catherine will sail for Varna on the next tide. You can take a household abroad, or a box, or no one. You can stay and make a stand. Each is a way to be at the end of the road, and each has a price.

options.label: Hold Carfax to the last night with the servants you have left.
options.detail: Make a stand in the chapel. Strong walls and one door, with no way out.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is at Carfax, my friends, with all he has left. We shall go in at noon.

options.outcome: You gather your servants, your boxes, and what is left of your strength in the old chapel. The hunters will come by day. It is a fine place to wait: it has stone walls and a single door, and the whole history of a house to be defended.

options.label: Arrange a household's passage abroad: Mina, Renfield, and the others, under false names.
options.detail: Eight places on a steamer for Antwerp, in four names. A court abroad.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: Eight passengers and a quantity of baggage, Count. It is a great deal of trouble for a foreign gentleman.

options.outcome: You take passage for eight on a steamer for Antwerp, in four names, with boxes of earth and a trunk of old gold. It is a large undertaking and you carry it out with patience. The ship leaves on a Tuesday.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS A HOLD ON THOSE YOU HAVE MARKED

options.label: Book the Czarina Catherine for one, with one box, and go home.
options.detail: Give up the court and go home alone with one box.

quote.speaker: Lloyd's agent
quote.text: A single box and a single gentleman for Varna, sir. We have no passengers, but I dare say the captain can find you a berth.

options.outcome: The Czarina Catherine is a plain steamer with a plain captain and a hold of general cargo. You take a berth under another name and go aboard at dusk with one large box. London falls behind you. You learned a good deal of it, and not enough.

echoes.text: The court is gone, and the house is quiet.
Carfax belongs to a trust, and the hunters have had to find a magistrate.

19B.title: What a Court Is Made Of
19B.description: The court has been tried and has been found to be made of people. Some of them are gone, and some are afraid, and one or two, at the last, are still on your side. The hunters are at the door or at the quay. There is a road home and a road through London, and a third, which you have not allowed yourself to think about. Whatever you choose now will be said about you for a long time, by people who never knew you.

options.label: Take your household abroad: the marked, the faithful and the boxes, to a house in another country.
options.detail: Move the household abroad on the ebb. The hunters will search the ships too late.

quote.speaker: Servant
quote.text: We are very comfortable, Master. It is a pleasant house, in a pleasant country. Nobody asks us anything.

options.outcome: You book eight places in four names, and the household goes aboard by lantern: the marked, the faithful, a trunk of old gold and the boxes. The master of the steamer asks nothing.

options.label: Take Mina with you, home, by the road.
options.detail: Take Mina with you on the Czarina Catherine. The hunters follow by another ship.

quote.speaker: Jonathan
quote.text: Mina is not there, Quincey. Her room is open and her bed is made. I think he has taken her.

options.outcome: You find her at the quay where you told her to wait, awake and silent. She looks at the ship, and at you, and goes aboard without asking where the boxes are.

options.label: Hold Carfax to the end, with the servants you have left.
options.detail: Stay and hold Carfax with whoever remains. The hunters will come at noon.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Mr Harker, go round by the chapel. I will take the door. Ma'am, you stay behind the Doc.

options.outcome: You send Billington's clerks away with the keys, light the lamps, and wait in the chapel. The servants come into the hall one by one and do not ask what you intend.

options.label: Release them: the marked, the faithful, all of them. Go home alone.
options.detail: Set every servant free and go home alone.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: He let us go. He stood in the hall and he told us we could go. I do not know what it cost him. I think it cost a great deal.

options.outcome: You call them into the hall one night: the servants, the marked, the creatures, and Renfield in his nightshirt. You have not asked anything of them for a long time.
options.requiresHint: OPENS TO WHAT YOUR EARLIER CHOICES HAVE MADE OF YOU

echoes.text: Carfax is full of servants, and every lamp is lit.

12C.title: A Wolf, Some Rats and a Fog
12C.description: Every animal in London can hear you. It is a thing you had forgotten until you stood in the garden at Carfax on the third night and said a word you have not said since the pass. A grey wolf in a cage in Regent's Park lifted his head. Behind every skirting-board in the Borough something stopped gnawing. Down on the river a bank of fog began, very slowly, to turn round. You have a good many instruments and you have not yet decided which to take up first.

options.label: Call the old wolf and hold him on a short lead: he will be your hand.
options.detail: Hold the wolf close as your hand. It is hard work, and he may bolt.

quote.speaker: Zookeeper
quote.text: He was always the quietest wolf in the Gardens. I cannot account for it, sir. He simply went through the bars.

success.outcome: The old grey wolf goes out through the bars of his cage as if they were water. He comes across the Heath at your heel, quiet and attentive and large. You tell him what you want, and he understands.

failure.outcome: The wolf will not come to heel. He goes across the Heath on his own account, and a policeman at Hampstead sees a grey shape the size of a calf go over a wall with something in its jaws. You hear about it in the morning, with the other news.

options.label: Call every rat in London, and let the wolf run where he likes.
options.detail: Rats in every wall of London move on Purfleet. The wolf runs where he likes.

quote.speaker: Sanitary inspector
quote.text: I never saw so many, sir. Not in the Docks. They came up out of the sewers in the dark, and they all went one way.

options.outcome: They come out of the sewers by the thousand, grey and patient, and move towards Purfleet like water running downhill. The wolf goes his own way across the Heath. You do not know where he is, and do not much mind.

options.label: Call the fog first, and keep the animals in reserve. The wolf will find his own way out.
options.detail: Raise the fog first. It costs a night of strength and holds as long as you wish.

quote.speaker: Policeman
quote.text: Never seen anything like it. A fog in September, in a clear sky, and it will not move. It stands in the lane like a wall.

options.outcome: You go up onto the chapel roof and lift your hands. The fog begins to rise from the river and creep through the streets of Purfleet. It will stay as long as you wish, and it will cost you a night of strength to start it. The wolf, behind the Heath, has come out of his cage on his own account.

13C.title: The Asylum Under Siege
13C.description: The fog has been in Purfleet for three days. Dr Seward and his friends are gathering in the house next to Carfax: the young men with their guns, the old professor with his bag, and in an upper room a young woman with a typewriter. You stand at the wall at night and look at the lit windows. Every one of them is afraid, and every one of them is sitting up. The question is how much of a siege you intend to make, and how long you can afford to keep it.

options.label: Send the rats into the walls of the asylum: let them hear it in the plaster.
options.detail: Rats in the walls of the asylum. The house will not sleep.

quote.speaker: Dr Seward
quote.text: The rats are in the walls and under the floor, and in the study. I have had the house inspected. It is entirely sound. I do not know what they want.

options.outcome: The rats go in at every drain and gutter. By the second night every wall in the house is full of scratching, and the doctor has taken to sleeping on the stair with a shotgun. In the morning the old professor looks at the plaster and says nothing.

options.label: Bring the fog to the doorstep and keep it there: let them be afraid of the garden.
options.detail: Lay fog over the garden. Hunting stops in it, and it costs you each night.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: I cannot see my own gun, Doc. I do not like it. A man could walk straight up to you and you would not know until he spoke.

options.outcome: You lay the fog in the garden like a cold hand, and the garden empties. The horses will not come up the lane. For three nights the asylum is a ship in a grey sea and the people in it do not sleep. It works, and it costs you.

options.label: Do nothing for three nights. Let them wonder.
options.detail: Do nothing for three nights. They will sit up listening to silence.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: Nothing came last night, Seward. I do not trust nothing. A wolf that does not howl is a wolf that is waiting.

options.outcome: You go to ground for three nights and keep the animals still. The hunters sit up and listen to silence. By the third night one of them has fallen asleep at his post, and the old man is looking at him with the expression of a general who has just found his sentry drunk.

echoes.text: The wolf is at your heel. He has not been told to hurry.
The rats of London are in Purfleet. You can feel them like a rash on the city.
The fog is your servant and will stay as long as you can afford it.
The wolf is somewhere on the Heath on his own account.

14C.title: The Window at Hillingham
14C.description: On a hill in Hampstead stands a house called Hillingham, where a girl called Lucy Westenra is ill and her mother sits up with her. The old professor has put garlic on the window, and the window is bolted. It has not kept the girl from sleeping, and it will not keep a wolf from the glass. A house in which the mother is awake is a house in which the child is not alone. You have a choice of ways in, and none of them is kind.

options.label: Send the wolf through the window, and take what you came for in the confusion.
options.detail: The wolf breaks in while you feed. You come away stronger, and the house comes after you.

quote.speaker: Zookeeper
quote.text: He put his head through the glass as if it were paper, and the mother died of the shock. I never knew such a thing.

options.outcome: The wolf goes through the window at midnight in a shower of glass. The mother, in her chair, has time to rise and no more. In the confusion you take what you came for. You are much stronger afterwards, and you will not think about what you have done.

options.label: Come as a mist at the keyhole, and leave the wolf where he is.
options.detail: Come through the keyhole as a mist and take only a little. The house does not wake.

quote.speaker: Lucy
quote.text: I dreamed there was a mist in the room. It came in at the key-hole. It was very cold, and it was kind.

options.outcome: You come through the lock as a long grey breath and take only what the girl can spare. She lies in bed with the flowers about her and smiles in her sleep. The mother, in her chair, does not wake. In the morning there is a mist on the window and a girl who is a little paler than she was.

options.label: Leave the girl to the doctors. You have a larger siege.
options.detail: A girl in Hampstead is a distraction. The enemy is in Purfleet.

quote.speaker: Arthur
quote.text: I do not know what Seward thinks the matter is. I believe she is a little better. She ate a little supper last night.

options.outcome: You turn your face to Purfleet. The girl at Hillingham, whom nothing now threatens, sits up in bed and eats a little supper. Her suitors send flowers. She does not know that she was ever chosen, and that she was then released.

echoes.text: You marked her at Whitby, on the bench, and she has been waiting for you.
The walls of the asylum are alive with scratching.
They have been sitting up in silence for three nights, and are tired of it.

15C.title: The Garlic and the Cross
15C.description: The old man from Amsterdam has taken command. He has put up garlic on every window at Purfleet, a cross on every door, and a silver box of small white wafers in the pocket of his coat. He is patient, unflinching and well read. His friends are afraid of him in the way that men are afraid of a surgeon who is going to save them. You have a good many animals and he has a good many flowers. The next move is yours, and he will not be fooled twice.

options.label: Strike at the old man himself: he is the brain of them.
options.detail: Go for Van Helsing himself, at his window. He is the one who knows.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He came to my window last night, Seward, in the shape of a fog. I was not afraid. I have known fear, and this was a very different thing.

success.outcome: You go to him as a grey breath on the glass and, for the length of a breath, you reach him. His mind is old and orderly and shut like a library. You take a little of his strength and he takes a great deal more of your measure. When he speaks one word of Latin you retreat, but not before you have learned what he fears.

failure.outcome: Garlic on the sill, and the old man awake behind it.

options.label: Go to the asylum by night and try the old man's bread at a door, to learn what it does.
options.detail: Touch the wafer at a doorway and learn exactly what it does. It will hurt, and he will see the mark.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A burn, Seward, on the door, in the shape of a hand. I could not have devised a better experiment myself.

options.outcome: You lay your palm against the door where he has set the wafer. The pain is quite unlike anything you have felt, and it lasts for a night. You know now what it does and how far it reaches, and so does he. The mark on the wood is in the shape of a hand.

options.label: Ignore him. Go for the young men's nerves.
options.detail: Work on the young men's nerves instead. A frightened friend is a poor ally.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: I am not a nervous man, Doc. But I cannot say I like the way the shadows have been behaving.

options.outcome: You go round the house at night and put a thought into the window of each young man in turn: a small cold fear, a footstep on the stair, the sense of being looked at. They do not sleep. Within a week they are quarrelling, and the old man is spending the days keeping them together.

options.label: Send the old professor a perfectly courteous card proposing a meeting: unsettle him with civility.
options.detail: A calling card in your best hand. Courtesy from you may unsettle him more than fear.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: A card, Seward, from the gentleman at Carfax, in a very good hand. He asks me to dine. I begin to think that he is laughing at us.

options.outcome: You write it on your best paper, in a hand that has not changed in centuries. A servant of Lord Godalming brings it up at breakfast. The old man reads it three times and puts it in his pocket. He does not reply. For two days he is very quiet, and his friends do not know what to make of it.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF MANNERS

options.label: Read the old man's own paper on the subject in a library. A doctor's habit, and cheaper than a burnt hand.
options.detail: He will have written it down. Men of his sort always do.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: I wrote a paper once for the Medical Society of Amsterdam. Nobody read it. I did not think anyone ever would.

options.outcome: You find it in the library of a medical society in Bloomsbury, bound in grey cloth and uncut. It is thirty pages on the effect of consecrated bread on the unquiet dead. It is careful and exact. You know what the old man knows, and he does not know that you know it.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF DOCTORS

echoes.text: You came to the girl as a mist, and she smiled in her sleep.
The girl at Hillingham is eating her supper, and does not know she was spared.

16C.title: The Night Visit at Purfleet
16C.description: At one in the morning the attendant finds a patient lying on the floor of his room with his head broken. Upstairs in the same house a young woman sleeps with her husband beside her, in a sleep that is not his own. She is the one who types. In the grey room where the papers are kept she has made a good account of you. She has also, with a sort of fair-minded courage, put your side of it. It is very late and the fog is at the window. What you do in this room will decide a good deal.

options.label: Take her, with her husband beside her in a stupor.
options.detail: Take Mina with Jonathan asleep beside her. The hunters will come for the house.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: I woke with the taste of salt and iron in my mouth, and a man bending over me, and I could not call out.

options.outcome: Jonathan sleeps beside her without stirring. She wakes as you bend to her and does not cry out, and for a long minute it is only the two of you. You take what you need of her. When the house stirs you go by the window, and the last thing you hear is her voice, steady, saying her husband's name.

options.label: Come to her through the fog, and speak to her. Show her what you are.
options.detail: Show her what you are and let her decide what it means. She may help you, or write you down.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: He stood at the foot of the bed and spoke very quietly. I do not remember all of it. I remember he did not touch me.

options.outcome: You come in as a thin grey mist and take your own shape in the corner of the room. She sits up and looks at you. You speak very quietly, in your best English. She does not cry out. When you have finished, you go out of the window as you came, and she goes back to her typewriter.

options.label: Take her husband's journal and her typescript, and leave her alone. Her papers are your danger.
options.detail: Take the journal, the typescript and the carbon. She keeps her life, and they lose their map.

quote.speaker: Mina
quote.text: The typescript was on the desk, Jonathan. It is gone. The whole of it, and your journal. I do not think it was a burglar.

options.outcome: You take the journal, the typescript and the carbon, and fold the pages into your coat. The woman at the desk does not wake. You could have done a great deal more, and she will not forgive even this.

echoes.text: Her husband never came home. She is typing from the Demeter's log and a few letters.
Lucy's mother is dead, and the house at Hillingham is in mourning. Mina has been there for three days.
The old man looked you in the face and said a word in Latin.
The young men are quarrelling, and the old man is keeping them together.
The old man has a page that says what you did in the order you did it.
The old man tells his friends he has driven you off. He does not believe it.
Every one of the young men has felt something at his window.
The old man has your card in his pocket, and has not replied.
You know what the old man knows, and he does not know that you know it.

17C.title: The Siege of Carfax
17C.description: They come at noon, five men and a locksmith, with a cart of bread and flowers. You are in the chapel in your box with the lid down. Your animals are outside, and the fog has not yet lifted. You hear Lord Godalming open the door of the house, because it is his right to open any door. The old man is on his knees in the dust of the nave with a silver box. Somewhere in the garden a rat is crying like a child. The first of your beds goes dead like a tooth.

options.label: Fight: the rats at the doors, the wolf in the garden, and the fog in the lane.
options.detail: You have never been so strong, and they have never been so few.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Mr Harker, mind the left. The Doc has the door. Ma'am, stay behind the Doc.

options.outcome: The rats come out of the walls and the wolf comes round the end of the chapel. For ten minutes the nave is a battle: the old man's wafers, the young men's guns, the locksmith's crowbar. The hunters hold the door. You are unhurt, and the house is lost.

options.label: Move the boxes in the fog, by night, to the next lair.
options.detail: You know the streets. A cart in a fog is no more than a cart.

quote.speaker: Carter
quote.text: Eleven boxes in one night, sir, in a fog so thick I could not see my own horse. I do not like it. I will do it for the money.

options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE CITY

success.outcome: You work through the night with a hired cart and a driver who will not look back. In the fog a cart is only a shadow: the lamps are yellow smears, the streets are a long corridor. By dawn eleven boxes are in a cellar in Mile End and Carfax is empty.

failure.outcome: The fog thins before the work is done. A policeman on his beat sees a cart at the end of a lane with its tarpaulin half off, and a gentleman in a long coat beside it. He writes it in his notebook, and you have six boxes left on the pavement.

options.label: Abandon Carfax and bring the storm to the next lair.
options.detail: Leave the chapel and its boxes. Take the storm to the next lair.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: They are sealed, my friends, every one of them. We have closed a door in his house. There are others.

options.outcome: You leave the chapel by the crypt and go across the fields in the shape of a wolf. The hunters seal the chapel and the boxes in it, and are content. You watch from beyond the wall. You have other houses, and plenty of fog.

options.label: Have Billington and Son serve notice: the chapel is private property, and the hunters are trespassers.
options.detail: Four hours of lawyers are four hours of night.

quote.speaker: Mr Billington
quote.text: I have the honour to inform you that you are trespassing, my lord. I should be obliged if you would withdraw.

options.outcome: A clerk in a bowler hat arrives at noon with a paper and a formal manner. Lord Godalming reads it twice. For the next four hours the hunters are lawyers, and the old man is heard to say several things in Dutch. It is a small delay. You use it.
options.requiresFlagHint: NEEDS WHAT MR HARKER TAUGHT YOU OF THE LAW

echoes.text: She heard you out, and did not scream.
Her typescript is in your coat, and the carbon with it.

18C.title: Flight in a Gale
18C.description: Carfax is sealed and the list of your lairs is a shorter list than it was. At Lloyd's a steamer called the Czarina Catherine is advertised for Varna on the next tide. The hunters will be at the quay, or on the next boat, or on the road at the other end. There is a way to cover a departure that has never been tried in the Thames: a storm. You have the strength to raise a small one. You have, perhaps, not the strength to raise a large one.

options.label: Raise a gale on the Channel to cover the voyage: a storm the hunters cannot follow.
options.detail: Raise a gale to cover the sailing. It costs you dearly, and the hunters cannot follow.

quote.speaker: Captain
quote.text: I have been twenty years at sea, and I never saw a gale come up like that. It was like a hand.

success.outcome: The wind comes round to the south-west in an hour and the glass falls like a stone. By midnight the Channel is a white field and no pilot will take a boat out. The Czarina Catherine goes down the river before it, with her hold shut and her captain wondering at his luck. You have not been so tired in years.

failure.outcome: The wind comes, and it will not be told when to stop. For two nights the Channel is a place of wreckage and rope. The steamer is forced back into Gravesend and loses a day. When she goes out again, it is on a clear night, and there are men on the pier.

options.label: Take the Czarina Catherine quietly with one box, and let the fog carry you down the river.
options.detail: A lesser instrument than the gale, and cheaper. The steamer goes down the Thames unseen.

quote.speaker: Lloyd's agent
quote.text: A single box for Varna, sir. We have no passengers, but I dare say the captain can find you a berth.

options.outcome: You take a berth under another name and go aboard at dusk with one large box. The fog is on the river and the captain is glad of it. The steamer goes down the Thames at a walking pace, and the quays cannot see her.

options.label: Stay. Finish the old man first.
options.detail: Kill the old man before you leave. The plan is good, and the risk is high.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is not leaving, my friends. He is coming for me. I knew he would. I only hoped he would not do it so soon.

options.outcome: You decide not to run. The old man is the brain of them, and the brain can be taken. You spend the last night in London planning. It is a good plan, and a bad idea, and you carry it out with great energy.

echoes.text: Carfax is sealed, and you feel each of its beds as a dead tooth.
You held the chapel for ten minutes and lost the house.
A policeman has written down a cart in a lane, and a gentleman in a long coat.
The hunters spent an afternoon as lawyers.

19C.title: The Fog or the Road
19C.description: There is a road home, and there is a road through London. There is a third, which you have been reluctant to think of: to be, at last, the thing you were made to be. The hunters are at your heels. The fog is thinning and your animals are weary. Behind you is a city that has begun to learn what you are. Ahead is a pass in the Carpathians, a castle, and a long night.

options.label: Go home on the gale: the storm you raised, and the steamer in it.
options.detail: Sail on the gale you raised. The hunters cannot follow into it.

quote.speaker: Captain
quote.text: We made Varna in six days, sir, with the wind on our quarter all the way. I never saw the like.

options.outcome: The steamer takes you on at dusk with one box in the hold, and the gale you raised is waiting for her at the Nore.

options.label: Go back to Purfleet and finish it: the old man first, and then the rest.
options.detail: Return to Purfleet and strike at the old man. It may end the hunt, or you.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is at the gate, my friends, with every beast in London. We have bread and flowers and each other. It will have to do.

options.outcome: You send the fog ahead of you like a scout, call the rats out of the Borough, and wait for the lamps at Purfleet to be lit.

options.label: Travel by night only, with your wolves, and take the long road home.
options.detail: Travel by night only, by farm cellars, with the wolves for scouts. Slow, and hard to follow.

quote.speaker: Szgany headman
quote.text: We have waited for you three weeks, master. The pass is open. The sisters have the lamp lit.

options.outcome: You settle the last accounts with Billington and Son, and arrange for the wolves to meet you in Kent.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS ENOUGH STRENGTH TO TRAVEL BY NIGHT

options.label: Stay. Make London learn what you are.
options.detail: Stay and turn London's fear into a siege. It costs you everything, and the city remembers.

quote.speaker: Policeman
quote.text: I have been on the Embankment for twenty years. I never saw a fog like it, and I never heard so many dogs.

options.outcome: At dusk you climb the chapel at Carfax and lift both hands. Every instrument you own is awake.
options.requiresHint: NEEDS ENOUGH TERROR IN YOUR PAST, AND ENOUGH STRENGTH IN YOUR PRESENT

echoes.text: The Channel was a place of wreckage, and the steamer lost a day.
You have decided not to run.

10-X.title: The Old Man Saw
10-X.description: You were seen. The old man who sits on the bench every evening was walking home by the Abbey wall when the fair girl came out in her nightdress, and he stopped in the lane with his stick and watched a tall man in a dark coat take her hand. He has said nothing yet. In the morning he will be on the seat again with his pipe, telling anyone who will listen what walks in the churchyard. Most of Whitby has stopped listening to him. The coastguard has not.

options.label: Let him talk. Nobody believes an old man on a bench.
options.detail: Leave the old man to his story. Whitby has heard it before.

quote.speaker: Old Mr Swales
quote.text: There be things that walk this churchyard, miss, and I have seen the tallest of them.

options.outcome: He tells it to the coastguard, the doctor and the curate. The coastguard writes it down. The doctor says that he is old. By the end of the week it is the town's favourite story, and not a word of it is believed.

options.label: Be on the seat before him, in the dark, and wait.
options.detail: He sits there every morning at six. He has never once looked behind him.

quote.speaker: Coastguard
quote.text: I took my cap off before I would touch him, sir. I never saw a man look so frightened, and his neck was broken.

options.outcome: The coastguard finds him at six, on the seat with his face to the sea and his neck broken. The doctor says he fell. The coastguard takes off his cap and does not say what he thinks. You are on the railway by evening, and you are not proud of it.

options.label: Leave Whitby tonight, by the first train south.
options.detail: Take the milk train south with the boxes. Whitby was never going to be home.

quote.speaker: Porter
quote.text: A foreign gentleman? He took the milk train, sir, and never said a word.

options.outcome: You take the milk train with the boxes in the van. Behind you the old man sits on his bench in the early light, telling it to the gulls. The platform did not look at you.

12B-X.title: A Gaffe at Dinner
12B-X.description: The dinner is in Belgrave Square, and the fish has not yet gone round when it happens. A footman bends to fill your glass and you do not move, and you do not move for so long that the lady on your left looks from your face to your plate and back. You have eaten nothing. You have said so three times. She has begun to tell the man on her other side.

options.label: Laugh, and say that you keep the hours of your own country.
options.detail: A story about the table manners of your own country. It has to be amusing.

quote.speaker: Lady on your left
quote.text: A foreign custom, Lord Henry. They dine at very odd hours in the East.

options.outcome: You tell a long story about a dinner in a mountain castle at which the host was served last. It is a good story, and she laughs in the right places. By the cheese she has decided that you are a charming eccentric. The man on her other side has not.

options.label: Take a mouthful of fish and a glass of wine, and bear it.
options.detail: It will be a bad quarter of an hour. It will also be over.

quote.speaker: Footman
quote.text: The Count took the claret, my lady, and he took a little of the sole.

options.outcome: The fish is the worst thing you have tasted in a long life, and the wine is not much better. You keep it down until you reach your carriage. You do not dine out for a week, and the table remembers nothing but your manners.

options.label: Make your excuses before the second course and leave.
options.detail: Leave before the second course. You are remembered as delicate, not as strange.

quote.speaker: Hostess
quote.text: He was taken ill, I am afraid. He bowed to me very prettily on the stair. I do not think he will come again.

options.outcome: You take your hat from the footman and your leave from the hostess, in that order. In the street you stand under a lamp and breathe the fog. By morning the whole of Belgrave Square knows that the foreign gentleman is delicate.

16A-X.title: They Were Waiting
16A-X.description: The first man through the door is not alone. Dr Seward's friends have posted a watcher in the crypt with a lantern and a cross, a plain young man in a coat too big for him, and he has stayed awake all night. He lifts the cross as you come at him out of the dark, and for a moment you have nothing to say. The others come up behind him with the old man and his silver box. They knew that you would be here. It is the first time that anyone has.

options.label: Go back into the walls as a mist, and give them the empty crypt.
options.detail: Give them the empty crypt. The old man will feel you there all the same.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He was here, my friends. The air is cold as a church. He has gone into the wall like a draught.

options.outcome: You pour yourself into a crack in the stone as a cold draught, and lie in the wall for an hour. The old man walks the crypt with a candle and says that he can feel you. He is right. He lays a wafer on every ledge he can reach, and you lie in the dark between two stones and do not move.

options.label: Send the rats to the lantern and the wolf to the stair, and go in the confusion.
options.detail: A watcher with a cross has one hand for the cross and one for the lantern. Take away the second.

quote.speaker: Watcher
quote.text: They were all over the floor. I dropped the lantern. I never saw so many, sir, and they were not afraid of the cross.

options.outcome: The rats come out of the walls and over the floor, and the lantern goes out. In the dark the wolf is on the stair. The young man drops the cross and the old man picks it up. By the time a match is struck you are in the garden, and the crypt is full of rats, and not a man has been hurt.

options.label: Stand where you are, and look the watcher in the face until the cross shakes.
options.detail: Hold the watcher's eyes until the cross shakes. It takes all you have.

quote.speaker: Watcher
quote.text: I could not move, sir. I could not lower my arm. I think I could have stood there until morning.

options.outcome: He holds the cross out at arm's length and it shakes like a reed. You hold his eyes. It takes everything you have, and when the old man puts a hand on the boy's shoulder, you are tired. The hunters have learned that there is something in the crypt that can be looked at and not looked away from.

15C-X.title: The Word in Latin
15C-X.description: You come to his window as a mist, and the flowers on the sill turn you back like a hand on a door. The old man sits up, opens the shutter and looks you in the face. He pronounces a single word of Latin, a short one, and it goes through you like cold water through a net. When you have gathered yourself in the garden you are lighter than you were, and he is writing in his notebook.

options.label: Send the rats to his room and the wolf under his window while he writes.
options.detail: Rats and a wolf for the night. He will write less, or write more.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: They are at the door and under the sill, Seward. It is exactly what he would do. I wrote it down before he did it.

options.outcome: The rats go up the pipes and the wolf lies down under the sill. The old man does not stop writing. Now and then he looks up, and says something in Dutch, and goes on. In the morning he has a page that says what you did, in the order you did it.

options.label: Withdraw into the fog, and let him think he has won.
options.detail: Retreat into the fog. Let Van Helsing think he has driven you off.

quote.speaker: Van Helsing
quote.text: He is gone, my friends. I do not believe it. A thing of that kind does not go away because it has been told to.

options.outcome: You go back to Carfax by the fields and lie down in your own earth. The old man tells his friends that he has driven you off. He does not believe it, and neither do you, and the quiet that follows is the most careful of the whole campaign.

options.label: Go round to the young men's windows instead. The old man cannot be at all of them.
options.detail: Go to the young men's windows. The old man cannot guard all of them.

quote.speaker: Quincey
quote.text: Something was at my window, Doc. I did not see it. I felt it the way you feel a rattlesnake in the dark.

options.outcome: You go from window to window with the fog at your back. The old man cannot be at all of them, and he is not. By morning every one of the young men has felt something, and the only thing they can agree on is that they would rather not discuss it.

LORE_LETTER.headline: A LETTER ABOUT A HOUSE AT PURFLEET
LORE_LETTER.bodyText:
To Count Dracula, Castle Dracula, near the Borgo Pass.

Dear Sir, I am glad to report that the purchase of the house at Purfleet is complete. The property is an old one, of considerable extent, and stands in its own grounds behind a high stone wall. It has a small chapel, a good deal of land and very few neighbours. On one side is a private asylum for the insane, which is quiet and well conducted.

My partner, Mr Harker, will wait upon you at the castle in the second week of May to settle the last of the papers. He is a young man of the utmost reliability. I hope you will find him a suitable companion.

I remain, dear Sir, your obedient servant.

LORE_GAZETTE.headline: A STORM ON THE COAST: A VESSEL ASHORE
LORE_GAZETTE.bodyText:
WHITBY. A storm of unusual violence struck this coast in the night, and on the evening tide a foreign schooner ran in under full canvas and went ashore on the sand below the churchyard. A large crowd collected on the cliff. The coastguard, who were quickly on the spot, report that she is a Russian vessel out of Varna, with a cargo of silver sand and some boxes of mould.

A number of residents say that a large dog was seen to leave the vessel at the moment of grounding and run up the Abbey steps. It has not been found. The coastguard asks that owners keep their dogs indoors.

LORE_ALMANACK.source: Notes in the margin of Whitaker's Almanack
LORE_ALMANACK.headline: WHAT THE BOOKS SAY OF ENGLAND
LORE_ALMANACK.bodyText:
The city has four millions of people, and a policeman on every corner who does not know one of them by name. A man may buy a house for gold in the afternoon and be a householder by evening. He may have a title, a club and a carriage on the strength of a letter from a solicitor. Nobody asks where a man's money comes from. Nobody asks where he sleeps.

The river runs to the sea, and the sea is open. There are a great many ships. In the whole of London, a man may be quite alone and quite unobserved for years, and be thought merely foreign. This is the country, and it is time to decide what to be in it.

LORE_WOLF.headline: AN ESCAPED WOLF: THE ZOOLOGICAL GARDENS ALARMED
LORE_WOLF.bodyText:
A grey wolf has escaped from the Zoological Gardens in Regent's Park. The animal, which has been quiet for years, was last seen at dusk going north across the Heath. The keeper says it went through the bars of its cage as if it had been called, and paid no attention to him at all.

Residents of Hampstead and Purfleet are asked to bolt their shutters. The Superintendent wishes it understood that the wolf is old, tame and generally a gentle creature, and that it is not in the habit of breaking into houses.

LORE_CZARINA.headline: THE CZARINA CATHERINE, FOR VARNA
LORE_CZARINA.bodyText:
ADVERTISED. The steamer Czarina Catherine, 1,200 tons, is advertised to sail from the Pool of London on the next tide for Varna, with general cargo and one consignment of earth in a single large case for forwarding to Galatz. Her master reports no passengers.

The agent at Varna has been informed that her arrival is expected a day ahead of her usual time. Nobody at Lloyd's can account for the wind.

CRISIS_STRENGTH.source: A Page from the Count's Own Notebook
CRISIS_STRENGTH.headline: HUNGER
CRISIS_STRENGTH.bodyText:
I have not fed in eleven days. The earth is cold under my back, and the lid, when I put my hand to it, is heavier than I remember. In the night I heard a man walk by in the lane, and I could have named his dinner. I did not go out. I am no longer sure I could.

There are old tales about men like me who lay down in their boxes and did not rise. I used to think them stories for children. I am beginning to think they were written by someone who had been tired.

CRISIS_SECRECY.source: The Daily Telegraph, Letters to the Editor
CRISIS_SECRECY.headline: A FOREIGN GENTLEMAN AT PURFLEET
CRISIS_SECRECY.bodyText:
Sir, I write as a resident of Purfleet of nineteen years' standing. For some weeks a house near my own, long empty, has been occupied by a foreign gentleman whom nobody has seen to enter or leave. Carts come in the night. Dogs howl. A constable of my acquaintance tells me that a man passed through a locked gate in his presence and was not there when he turned round.

I do not wish to alarm your readers. I should like to know whether the police have made any inquiry. I am, Sir, your obedient servant, Pro Bono Publico.

CRISIS_DOMINION.headline: RENFIELD
CRISIS_DOMINION.bodyText:
PURFLEET. Renfield is quiet again. For three weeks he raved about a Master, and watched the lane from his window, and kept a count of sparrows. Tonight he sat on the edge of his bed with his hands in his lap and said that nobody was coming. He did not weep. I find that I mind it more than the raving.

I have also noticed that the animals at the gate have gone. The fog has lifted. The house next door has been dark for nine nights. I am an educated man and I do not believe in influence, and I am very much afraid that something has let go.

LORE_DEMETER_LOG.source: The Log of the Demeter: Varna to Whitby
LORE_DEMETER_LOG.headline: FOUND IN A BOTTLE
LORE_DEMETER_LOG.bodyText:
A bottle, carefully corked, was found in the dead man's pocket. In it was a roll of paper, the addendum to the ship's log. It was read to the inquest through a clerk of the Russian consul, who put it into English.

The hand is steady at first and grows worse. The crew are uneasy about the boxes of earth in the hold. A man is reported missing from the watch, and nobody can account for it. A second goes, and then a third. The mate is wild-eyed and cannot be calmed.

At the last the master was found lashed to the wheel, so that the ship should come into port with a hand upon her.

LORE_PHONO_RENFIELD.source: Dr Seward's Diary, kept in the phonograph
LORE_PHONO_RENFIELD.headline: R. M. RENFIELD, AGED FIFTY-NINE
LORE_PHONO_RENFIELD.bodyText:
Sanguine temperament. Great physical strength. Morbidly excitable, with periods of gloom that end in some fixed idea which I cannot make out.

He keeps flies, and spiders to eat the flies, and he is very careful of them. I think him a possibly dangerous man, and I have written down everything he says. I shall be glad to be wrong.

LORE_MINA_WHITBY.headline: ON THE EAST CLIFF
LORE_MINA_WHITBY.bodyText:
Lucy was out of bed again in the night, and this time I could not find her. I found her at last on our seat on the East Cliff, with the moon behind the abbey. There was something long and black bending over her, and it raised its head when I called her name.

She remembers nothing. I fastened her shawl at the throat with a big safety-pin, and I fear I was clumsy with it, for there are two little red points on her skin like pin-pricks. I have promised not to say a word to her mother.

Jonathan has not written for a long time.

LORE_SEWARD_LETTER.source: Dr Seward to the Hon. Arthur Holmwood
LORE_SEWARD_LETTER.headline: A LETTER ABOUT MISS WESTENRA
LORE_SEWARD_LETTER.bodyText:
My dear Art,

Miss Westenra is no better, and I cannot find the cause. I have written to an old friend and master of mine, Professor Van Helsing of Amsterdam, who knows as much about obscure diseases as any man living. I have asked him to come at once.

I shall see Miss Westenra again to-morrow. She is to meet me at the stores, so that I may not alarm her mother.

Yours always,
John Seward

LORE_BLOOFER.headline: A HAMPSTEAD MYSTERY
LORE_BLOOFER.bodyText:
The neighbourhood of Hampstead is much exercised by a series of events. Children have been missed, always late in the evening, and have come home next morning with very little account of themselves. The consensus of their excuses is that they had been with a “bloofer lady.”

The police are asked to keep a close look-out for straying children in and around Hampstead Heath, especially the very young, and for any stray dog which may be about.

LORE_TYPESCRIPT.headline: THE PAPERS, IN ORDER
LORE_TYPESCRIPT.bodyText:
MEMORANDUM. The papers are copied fair and set in order of date: Jonathan's journal from Exeter to the castle, Dr Seward's diary, spoken into the phonograph and written out from the cylinders, and my own. Where an entry is in shorthand I have put it into longhand. I have taken three copies of each.

Nothing is explained. I have set the dates side by side and let them say what they say.

ENDING_1A.title: A Quiet Neighbour
ENDING_1A.headline: THE HOUSE AT PURFLEET: STILL UNLET
ENDING_1A.text: You close the door of the last cellar and lie down in the last box. Over your head the hunt goes on for a month, and then for another. The old man searches Carfax, and the chapel, and the second house, and each time finds an empty room. Eventually he goes home to Amsterdam. You do not come out until the spring. London is large and has plenty to look at, and it looks at something else.

variants.headline: A GENTLEMAN OF PICCADILLY: THE RATEPAYER WHO WAS NEVER SEEN
variants.text: You close the door of the last cellar and lie down in the last box. Over your head the hunt goes on for a month, and then for another. The old man searches Carfax and the chapel, and finds nothing but a house with a clean title. In Piccadilly there is a ratepayer who has never been seen, and a deed in the strong-room of a firm of solicitors with no cause to open it. You come out in the spring. You are a quiet neighbour, in a large city, and you stay.

ENDING_1B.title: The Road Home
ENDING_1B.headline: STEAMER FOR VARNA LEAVES THE THAMES
ENDING_1B.text: The Czarina Catherine goes down the river on the ebb with one large box in her hold. The hunters are a quarter of an hour late at the quay. They stand on the pier and watch her go. At Varna the agent has the box on a lighter before the pilot has come aboard. You are in the castle, in your own earth, within the month. The door is open and the wind is in the corridors. It is quiet, and you are tired, and you are home.

variants.headline: THE SISTERS KEEP A PROMISE
variants.text: The Czarina Catherine goes down the river on the ebb with one large box in her hold, and reaches Varna ahead of anyone who might want to meet her. You are in the castle within the month. The door is open and the wind is in the corridors, and the three in the east wing are waiting at the gate. They have not forgotten what you promised them. They are patient and they are fond of you, and the winter is a long one.

ENDING_1C.title: The Last Sunset
ENDING_1C.headline: FOREIGN NOBLEMAN DIES IN THE CARPATHIANS
ENDING_1C.text: You are in your box on a wagon on a road in the mountains, at the end of a clear day. The sun is on the rim of the pass. Five men come over the ridge, and behind them a woman with a typewriter. Somebody says your name. A long knife goes across your throat and a short one into your heart, and it hurts for as long as it takes to say so. Then the earth is over you, and you are dust. The woman writes afterwards that there was a look of peace on your face. You will never know whether she is right.

variants.headline: TWO MEN KILL A NOBLEMAN ON A WAGON
variants.text: You are in your box on a wagon on a road in the mountains, at the end of a clear day. Five men come over the ridge, but the young solicitor is not one of them, because you did not let him come home. A tall American has a bowie knife and a young lord has a hatchet. They do it between them, quickly, with very little ceremony. Then the earth is over you, and you are dust. There is nobody to write it down.

ENDING_1D.title: The Long Sleep
ENDING_1D.headline: A CASTLE IN THE CARPATHIANS FOUND UNOCCUPIED
ENDING_1D.text: You go home by the oldest road, and nobody follows. In the crypt of the old chapel the ten boxes are waiting, and the door is where you left it. You lie down in the nearest and draw the lid over you. You leave the key in the lock on the inside. For a long time there is nothing, and then there is more of it. The castle is empty. The wolves go down to the village. The sisters sleep in the east wing, and in the morning they find that you are not to be woken.

variants.headline: A SOLICITOR REMEMBERS A HOST
variants.text: You go home by the oldest road, and nobody follows. In the crypt the ten boxes are waiting. You lie down in the nearest and draw the lid over you, and the key stays in the lock on the inside. In the dark you think, as you have thought many times, of a young man at a window in the third week of May, with a bead of blood on his chin, and of the staircase. It is little to remember, and it is more than you thought you had kept.

ENDING_2A.title: A House of Many Rooms
ENDING_2A.headline: A COUNT FROM THE EAST TAKES A HOUSE IN ANTWERP
ENDING_2A.text: The steamer for Antwerp leaves on the ebb with eight passengers, four names and a great deal of baggage. The hunters reach the quay a quarter of an hour late. By the time they think to search the ships, you are in the Scheldt, under a name they do not know. In Antwerp there is a good house with a chapel. It has a long table, which you set every night for people who do not eat, and a hall, in which a servant stands at attention at every door. It is a court. It is a small and quiet one.

variants.headline: A LADY WHO TYPES, AT THE END OF A LONG TABLE
variants.text: The steamer for Antwerp leaves on the ebb with eight passengers, and among them a woman who does not speak. In Antwerp you set a long table every night. She sits at the end of it with her hands in her lap, and she types, in the evenings, a long account that you are not allowed to read. She has not forgiven you. She has not left. You have a court, and it has a historian, and the historian is not on your side.

ENDING_2B.title: Two to the Pass
ENDING_2B.headline: WOMAN RECOVERED UNHARMED FROM A MOUNTAIN ROAD
ENDING_2B.text: The voyage is long. She sits on the box in the hold for the whole of it, awake and silent, and you talk. By Biscay you have said more to her than to anyone for centuries. At Varna the road is long and behind you, on another ship, are five men with rifles. They reach the pass at dusk. Somebody says her name, and she does not answer. A long knife goes across your throat and a short one into your heart. As you go to dust, she puts her hand on the lid.

variants.headline: WOMAN FOUND ON A MOUNTAIN ROAD WITH A DEAD MAN'S HAND
variants.text: She had said she would think, and she thinks the whole of the voyage. At Varna the road is long, and behind you, on another ship, are five men with rifles. At the pass she stands up in the wagon and tells them to wait. They do not wait. You go to dust, with your hand in hers. She says afterwards that she did not know what she meant, and that she has not stopped asking.

ENDING_2C.title: The Court Falls
ENDING_2C.headline: ATTACK ON A HOUSE AT PURFLEET: MANY INJURED
ENDING_2C.text: They come at noon. The servants stand in the hall with their hands at their sides and do not run. You are in the chapel in the box, with a little of your strength and none of your hope. The hunters are not quick, and they are very thorough, and they have brought a great deal of bread. By evening the chapel is quiet and the hall is empty. Somewhere in the garden, a man in a nightshirt is crying for a bird.

variants.headline: A HOUSE LIT FROM CELLAR TO ROOF, AND THEN DARK
variants.text: They come at noon, and the house has been lit from cellar to roof for a week. The servants stand in the hall in a row. A great many of them are weeping, and none of them runs. You are in the chapel, in the box, with a little of your strength. The hunters are not quick, and they are very thorough. By evening the hall is empty and every lamp in the house has been put out, one by one, by a young woman with a taper.

ENDING_2D.title: The Release
ENDING_2D.headline: A FOREIGN GENTLEMAN LEAVES A HOUSE AT PURFLEET
ENDING_2D.text: You stand in the hall at Carfax and tell each of them they are free. Some weep. Some do not understand. A man in a nightshirt asks if he may have a bird. You open the doors and walk down the drive. In the morning the hall is empty and the house is cold. A woman in the house at Purfleet puts a hand to her forehead, as if something had been taken from it, and sits down. You go home alone. It is a long road, and a quiet one, and for the first time in centuries nobody is waiting at the end of it.

variants.headline: A MADMAN RETURNS TO HIS ASYLUM, UNREPENTANT
variants.text: You stand in the hall at Carfax and tell each of them they are free. The man you took out of the asylum asks whether he may have a bird. You say that he may have a great many, and that he must now find them himself. You open the doors and walk down the drive. Dr Seward finds his patient asleep on the steps of the asylum the next morning, in a nightshirt, with a sparrow in his hands. You go home alone, and the road is long.

ENDING_3A.title: Home on the Gale
ENDING_3A.headline: GREAT GALE IN THE CHANNEL: STEAMER REPORTED SAFE AT VARNA
ENDING_3A.text: The Czarina Catherine runs before the gale for six days. In Varna the agent has your box on a lighter before the pilot has put his foot on the quay. Up the river and over the pass nothing is in your way. The hunters arrive two weeks later and find an empty castle with the door open and a fire still lit in the hall. You are in the crypt, in your own earth, asleep. The wind has dropped, and nobody knows where you are.

variants.headline: AN ENGLISH SOLICITOR'S PENCIL MARK, ON A CASTLE WALL
variants.text: The Czarina Catherine runs before the gale for six days, and nothing is in your way up the river and over the pass. The hunters arrive two weeks later and find an empty castle with the door open. On the wall of the north room, in pencil, a young man has scratched a date and a line of shorthand. The old man copies it into his notebook. You are in the crypt, asleep, and you do not mind. You let him go, and he went home.

ENDING_3B.title: Cornered at Purfleet
ENDING_3B.headline: FIGHT AT A MADHOUSE: THE NOBLEMAN AND THE PROFESSOR
ENDING_3B.text: You come back to Purfleet in the dark with the wolf at your heel, the rats in the walls and the fog behind you. The house is lit. The old man is at the door with his silver box, and Dr Seward has a shotgun and Lord Godalming a lamp. It is a very short fight and neither side wins it. At dawn the fog lifts. You are in the chapel at Carfax with the lid half closed, and a long grey light is coming in at the door, and they are coming up the drive with the last of the bread.

variants.headline: A PROFESSOR'S EXPERIMENT, AND ITS CONCLUSION
variants.text: You come back to Purfleet with the wolf at your heel and the fog behind you. You know what the old man's bread does, because you have felt it on your palm. It is a very short fight, and when it is over you are in the chapel at Carfax with a hand that will not close. The old man comes up the drive with the last of his wafers. He says it was a good experiment. He says that he is sorry it has to end so.

ENDING_3C.title: The Pass by Night
ENDING_3C.headline: WOLVES SEEN ON THE ROAD FROM VARNA
ENDING_3C.text: You go home by night, by a road that is on no map, and sleep each day in a different farm cellar with the lid shut over you. The hunters follow the sea, the railway and the river. They do not follow the wolves. You reach the castle a week before they do. At the pass the old man draws a ring of white bread in the grass around a woman who holds a rifle she does not know how to use, and stays inside it all night. In the morning he goes into the castle with a stake and a hammer. He finds the three in the east wing. You feel them go.

variants.headline: THREE WOMEN FOUND IN A CHAPEL, WITH THEIR LOSS
variants.text: You go home by night, and the hunters follow the sea. At the pass, an old man and a woman sit all night in a ring of bread, and in the morning he goes into the castle with a stake and a hammer. He finds the three in the east wing. They are asleep, and well fed, and quite happy. You feel them go, one after another. You have done a thing that most of those who loved you will not forgive. You are alive, and alone, and you did not turn round.

ENDING_3D.title: The Sovereign of Fog
ENDING_3D.headline: LONDON UNDER FOG FOR NINE DAYS: CAUSE UNKNOWN
ENDING_3D.text: The fog thickens until you can touch it. Every dog, every rat, every wolf in the south of England is in the streets that night. The Thames freezes at its edges. People lock their doors, put out their lamps and do not go out. In the morning there is nothing to be seen but a fog, and a feeling of having been looked at. It goes on for nine days. By the tenth, London has learned a thing about itself, and has begun to talk about leaving. You stand on the roof of the chapel at Carfax, and the whole city is silent under your hand.

variants.headline: THE WOLVES OF LONDON: A POLICE INQUIRY
variants.text: The fog thickens until you can touch it, and every dog, rat and wolf in the south of England is in the streets that night. It is a remarkable thing to have a pack hunt for you: you have never needed it so little. The Thames freezes at its edges. In the morning there is only a fog and a feeling of having been looked at. It goes on for nine days. At the end of them, a great deal of London has left, and the rest keeps its lamps lit.

ENDING_CRISIS_STRENGTH.title: The Box Left Closed
ENDING_CRISIS_STRENGTH.headline: A CHEST IS OPENED IN A CELLAR AT NOON
ENDING_CRISIS_STRENGTH.text: You have taken too little and spent too much. A night comes when you reach for the lid and it does not move. You lie in the earth and hear the street above you, the carts, the footsteps and a church bell striking late. Nobody finds you for a week. On the eighth day somebody does. It is noon, and the lid comes up, and a woman with a typewriter looks down at what is in the box. The old man says a word in Latin. It is a very short one.

ENDING_CRISIS_SECRECY.title: The Hue and Cry
ENDING_CRISIS_SECRECY.headline: A FOREIGN GENTLEMAN HUNTED THROUGH THE EAST END
ENDING_CRISIS_SECRECY.text: Nobody has seen you in a month, and now everybody has. The newspapers have a drawing of you and the police have a description. A constable at Purfleet has seen a man go through a locked gate, and a cabman in Camden Town has seen a man with no reflection in the window of a shop. They come with torches and dogs and handbills. The old man says that you must be a very great fool, and he does not say it unkindly. The crowd is waiting at the gate of Carfax at dawn.

ENDING_CRISIS_DOMINION.title: Alone at Carfax
ENDING_CRISIS_DOMINION.headline: A HOUSE AT PURFLEET STANDS EMPTY, WITH ALL ITS DOORS OPEN
ENDING_CRISIS_DOMINION.text: One by one they let go. The servants you flattered go back to their own lives. The friends you made at dinner stop returning your letters. Renfield sits at his window and looks the other way, and the wolf will not come when you call. At the end you sit in the chapel at Carfax beside a single box, with a candle and nobody. There is no siege. The house has only ever held people who did not agree to be in it. The hunters walk in by the front door.
